Gluing methods for quantitative stability
of optimal transport maps
Méthodes de recollement pour la stabilité quantitative des applications de transport optimal

Cyril Letrouit Address: Cyril Letrouit. Université Paris-Saclay, CNRS, Laboratoire de mathématiques d’Orsay, 91405, Orsay, France Email address: cyril.letrouit@universite-paris-saclay.fr and Quentin Mérigot Address: Quentin Mérigot. Université Paris-Saclay, CNRS, Inria, Laboratoire de mathématiques d’Orsay, 91405, Orsay, France / DMA, École normale supérieure, Université PSL, CNRS, 75005 Paris, France / Institut universitaire de France (IUF) Email address: quentin.merigot@universite-paris-saclay.fr
Date: August 24, 2026
Abstract.

Nous établissons des bornes de stabilité quantitatives pour l’application de transport optimal quadratique TμT_{\mu} entre une densité de probabilité fixée ρ\rho et une mesure de probabilité μ\mu sur ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}. Sous des hypothèses générales sur ρ\rho, nous montrons que l’application μ↦Tμ\mu\mapsto T_{\mu} est bi-höldérienne, avec des exposants de Hölder indépendants de la dimension. La distance de transport optimal linéarisée W2,ρ​(μ,ν)=‖Tμ−Tν‖L2​(ρ)W_{2,\rho}(\mu,\nu)=\|T_{\mu}-T_{\nu}\|_{L^{2}(\rho)} est ainsi équivalente de façon bi-höldérienne à la distance de Wasserstein W2​(μ,ν)W_{2}(\mu,\nu), ce qui justifie son utilisation en pratique.

Nous établissons cette propriété dans les cas suivants : (i) pour toute densité log-concave ρ\rho à support plein dans ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}, ainsi que pour toute perturbation log-bornée de celle-ci ; (ii) pour ρ\rho bornée inférieurement et supérieurement sur un domaine de John (par exemple, sur un domaine lipschitzien borné), alors que le seul résultat antérieur de ce type supposait la convexité du domaine ; (iii) pour certaines familles importantes de densités de probabilité sur des domaines bornés, qui décroissent ou explosent de manière polynomiale au voisinage du bord. Concernant le caractère optimal du point (ii), nous fournissons également des exemples de domaines qui ne sont pas de John pour lesquels les potentiels de Brenier ne satisfont aucune estimation de stabilité höldérienne.

Nos preuves reposent sur des inégalités locales de variance pour les potentiels de Brenier dans de petits sous-ensembles convexes du support de ρ\rho, que nous recollons afin d’obtenir une inégalité de variance globale. Cet argument de recollement s’appuie sur deux stratégies distinctes, présentant un intérêt propre : l’une exploite les propriétés de la décomposition de Whitney dans les domaines bornés, l’autre repose sur la théorie spectrale des graphes.

1. Introduction

Let 𝒫2​(ℝd)\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) be the set of probability measures with finite second moment over ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}. Given two probability measures ρ,μ\rho,\mu in 𝒫2​(ℝd)\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d}), the optimal transport problem for the quadratic cost in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} consists in solving the minimization problem

infγ∈Γ⁡(ρ,μ)∫ℝd×ℝd‖x−y‖2​𝑑γ​(x,y)\inf_{\gamma\in\Gamma(\rho,\mu)}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{R}^{d}}\|x-y\|^{2}d\gamma(x,y) (1.1)

where Γ⁡(ρ,μ)\Gamma(\rho,\mu) is the set of couplings between ρ\rho and μ\mu, i.e., the set of probability measures γ\gamma over the product space ℝd×ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{R}^{d} with first marginal ρ\rho and second marginal μ\mu. More generally, considering the LpL^{p} cost, we define the pp-Wasserstein distance between ρ\rho and μ\mu as

Wp​(ρ,μ)=(infγ∈Γ⁡(ρ,μ)∫ℝd×ℝd‖x−y‖p​𝑑γ​(x,y))1/p.W_{p}(\rho,\mu)=\left(\inf_{\gamma\in\Gamma(\rho,\mu)}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{R}^{d}}\|x-y\|^{p}d\gamma(x,y)\right)^{1/p}.

In this paper, we focus on the quadratic optimal transport problem in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}, i.e., the case p=2p=2. A theorem of Brenier [12] asserts that if ρ\rho is absolutely continuous with respect to the Lebesgue measure, then a unique solution γ∈Γ⁡(ρ,μ)\gamma\in\Gamma(\rho,\mu) of (1.1) exists, and it is induced by a map T=∇ϕT=\nabla\phi, where ϕ:ℝd→ℝ\phi:\mathbb{R}^{d}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} is a convex function.

Definition 1.1 (Potentials and maps).

We fix a probability measure ρ∈𝒫2​(ℝd)\rho\in\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d}), which we assume to be absolutely continuous with respect to the Lebesgue measure and supported in 𝒳⊂ℝd\mathcal{X}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d}. Given μ∈𝒫2​(ℝd)\mu\in\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d}), we call

  • •

    Brenier map and denote by TμT_{\mu} the (unique) optimal transport map between ρ\rho and μ\mu;

  • •

    Brenier potential the unique lower semi-continuous convex function ϕμ∈L2​(ρ)\phi_{\mu}\in L^{2}(\rho) such that Tμ=∇ϕμT_{\mu}=\nabla\phi_{\mu} and ∫𝒳ϕμ​𝑑ρ=0\int_{\mathcal{X}}\phi_{\mu}d\rho=0 (this function is always uniquely defined in the setting of this paper, see for instance Section 3.3).

The problem addressed in the present paper is the following: ρ\rho being fixed, and knowing that μ\mu and ν\nu are close to one another in some Wasserstein distance, how far can TμT_{\mu} and TνT_{\nu} be at most (e.g., in L2​(ρ)L^{2}(\rho))? The stability of Brenier maps under variation of the measures is indeed fundamental from a mathematical viewpoint: it is closely related to the convergence of numerical approaches to solve optimal transport problems and justifies many of the applications of optimal transport.

Since we are dealing with the quadratic cost, the most natural distance on 𝒫2​(ℝd)\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) to consider is the 22-Wasserstein distance. To summarize, we are interested in quantitative stability bounds for the map μ↦Tμ\mu\mapsto T_{\mu} from (𝒫2​(ℝd),W2)(\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d}),W_{2}) to L2​(ρ)L^{2}(\rho), i.e., bounds of the form

‖Tμ−Tν‖L2​(ρ)≤C​W2​(μ,ν)q\|T_{\mu}-T_{\nu}\|_{L^{2}(\rho)}\leq CW_{2}(\mu,\nu)^{q} (1.2)

where the constant qq is universal, and in particular independent of dd. Although this is not essential (see Remark 1.5), we assume in our main results that the supports of μ,ν\mu,\nu are contained in a compact set 𝒴\mathcal{Y}; the constant CC may depend on this set 𝒴\mathcal{Y} (and on ρ\rho), but not on any other property of μ,ν\mu,\nu.

Some comments are in order. Firstly, it is well-known that the map μ↦Tμ\mu\mapsto T_{\mu} from (𝒫2​(ℝd),W2)(\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d}),W_{2}) to L2​(ρ)L^{2}(\rho) is continuous, see [13, Theorem 1.3]. Secondly, since (Tμ,Tν)#​ρ(T_{\mu},T_{\nu})_{\#}\rho is a coupling between μ\mu and ν\nu, this map is reverse Lipschitz, i.e., ‖Tμ−Tν‖L2​(ρ)≥W2​(μ,ν)\|T_{\mu}-T_{\nu}\|_{L^{2}(\rho)}\geq W_{2}(\mu,\nu). Thirdly, simple examples show that one cannot expect in general q>1/2q>1/2 in (1.2) (see [33, Section 4] or [45, Lemma 5.1]). It is also natural to seek for stability bounds on the Brenier potentials, in the form

‖ϕμ−ϕν‖L2​(ρ)≤C′​W2​(μ,ν)q′.\|\phi_{\mu}-\phi_{\nu}\|_{L^{2}(\rho)}\leq C^{\prime}W_{2}(\mu,\nu)^{q^{\prime}}. (1.3)

As we will see later, (1.3) implies a bound of the form (1.2).

Despite its important theoretical and practical interest, the quantitative stability of optimal transport maps has attracted attention only recently ([33], [27], [7], [43], [24], [25], [45]). Variants of this problem include quantitative stability for entropic optimal transport under perturbations of the measures ([26], [30], [17]) or of the regularization parameter ([24], [29]), for semi-discrete optimal transport ([4], [29]), or for more general costs ([48], [32]). We also mention [18] which studies the quantitative stability of Wasserstein barycenters.

One of the motivations for studying the stability of optimal transport maps is that for a fixed source probability density ρ\rho, the mapping μ↦Tμ\mu\mapsto T_{\mu} provides an embedding of (𝒫2​(ℝd),W2)(\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d}),W_{2}) to the Hilbert space L2​(ρ,ℝd)L^{2}(\rho,\mathbb{R}^{d}). This embedding, often called linearized optimal transport, allows one to apply the standard “Hibertian” statistical toolbox to measure-valued data such as grayscale images [56], [41], [5]. This embedding is always distance-increasing, and stability estimates such as (1.2) show that it is bi-Hölder continuous. In other words, the distance d⁡(μ,ν)=‖Tμ−Tν‖L2​(ρ)d(\mu,\nu)=\|{T_{\mu}-T_{\nu}}\|_{L^{2}(\rho)} preserves in a rough way the geometry associated to the Wasserstein distance. In dimension d=1d=1, the embedding μ↦Tμ\mu\mapsto T_{\mu} is an isometry, see for instance [54, Theorem 2.18].

Our starting point is the following result of [25]. Here as in the rest of the paper, constants denoted by Ca1,…,anC_{a_{1},\ldots,a_{n}} are non-negative constants which depend on a1,…,ana_{1},\ldots,a_{n}. Since the source measure ρ\rho lives in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}, constants depending on ρ\rho implicitly depend on dd.

Theorem 1.2 (Introduction of [25]).

Let 𝒳⊂ℝd\mathcal{X}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} be a compact convex set and ρ\rho be a probability density on 𝒳\mathcal{X}, bounded from above and below by positive constants. Let p>dp>d and p≥4p\geq 4. Assume that μ,ν∈𝒫2​(ℝd)\mu,\nu\in\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) have bounded pp-th moment, i.e. max⁡(∫ℝd‖x‖p​𝑑μ​(x),∫ℝd‖x‖p​𝑑ν​(x))≤Mp<+∞\max(\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\|x\|^{p}d\mu(x),\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\|x\|^{p}d\nu(x))\leq M_{p}<+\infty. Then

‖Tμ−Tν‖L2​(ρ)\displaystyle\|T_{\mu}-T_{\nu}\|_{L^{2}(\rho)} ≤Cρ,p,Mp​W1​(μ,ν)p6​p+16​d\displaystyle\leq C_{\rho,p,M_{p}}W_{1}(\mu,\nu)^{\frac{p}{6p+16d}}
‖ϕμ−ϕν‖L2​(ρ)\displaystyle\|\phi_{\mu}-\phi_{\nu}\|_{L^{2}(\rho)} ≤Cρ,p,Mp​W1​(μ,ν)12.\displaystyle\leq C_{\rho,p,M_{p}}W_{1}(\mu,\nu)^{\frac{1}{2}}. (1.4)

If μ,ν\mu,\nu are supported on a compact set 𝒴\mathcal{Y}, the Hölder exponent for the Brenier map is improved:

‖Tμ−Tν‖L2​(ρ)≤Cρ,𝒴​W1​(μ,ν)16.\|T_{\mu}-T_{\nu}\|_{L^{2}(\rho)}\leq C_{\rho,\mathcal{Y}}W_{1}(\mu,\nu)^{\frac{1}{6}}. (1.5)
Remark 1.3 (Comparison between W1W_{1} and W2W_{2}).

We note that since W1≤W2W_{1}\leq W_{2}, the estimates in the above theorems, as well as in all results of the present paper, imply a bi-Hölder behaviour of the map μ↦Tμ\mu\mapsto T_{\mu} on subsets of 𝒫2​(ℝd)\mathcal{P}_{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) with respect to both Wasserstein distances W1W_{1} and W2W_{2}.

Our purpose in this paper is to obtain similar stability results for much more general source probability measures ρ\rho. Along the way, we unveil a strong analogy between optimal transport stability estimates and some proofs of Poincaré(-Wirtinger) inequalities. We also provide an example of ρ\rho for which stability of Brenier potentials fails. All together, these results give a fairly general picture of the source measures ρ\rho for which quantitative stability of optimal transport potentials and maps may be expected to hold.

In all previous works on the subject (notably [7], [45], [25], [29, Section 4], [48]), convexity, compactness and upper and lower bounds on ρ\rho were used in a crucial way. Our results show that neither the compactness, nor the convexity of 𝒳\mathcal{X} are actually needed for stability to hold, and that the density ρ⁡(x)\rho(x) may also be allowed to tend to 00 or to +∞+\infty at some controlled rate, either for xx close to the boundary of 𝒳\mathcal{X} if 𝒳\mathcal{X} is bounded, or as |x|→+∞|x|\rightarrow+\infty if 𝒳\mathcal{X} is unbounded.

We prove that the exponents we obtain for the stability of Brenier potentials are sharp in some cases, see for instance Theorem 1.12 and Proposition 6.10. This is the first time that stability exponents are proved to be sharp: for instance it is not known whether the exponents 1/21/2 in (1.4) and 1/61/6 in (1.5) are sharp or not.

The proofs of our main results leverage domain decomposition techniques and spectral graph theory. The starting point of our investigations was the proof of [18, Proposition B.2] in which it was first noticed, although on the different problem of quantitative stability of Wasserstein barycenters, that convexity of the support of ρ\rho might not be necessary to prove quantitative stability bounds.

1.1. The log-concave case

We first establish stability estimates in the case where the source measure ρ\rho is a log-concave probability density on ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}, with support equal to ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}. As in the Holley-Stroock principle ([37, page 1185], [3, Proposition 4.2.7]), we are also able to deal with log-bounded perturbations of log-concave measures. Our first main result is the following:

Theorem 1.4.

Let ρ=e−U−F​d​x\rho=e^{-U-F}dx be a probability density on ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}, with D2​U≥κ⋅IdD^{2}U\geq\kappa\cdot{\rm Id} for some κ>0\kappa>0, and F∈L∞​(ℝd)F\in L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{d}). Let 𝒴⊂ℝd\mathcal{Y}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} be a compact set. Then, there exists Cρ,𝒴>0C_{\rho,\mathcal{Y}}>0 such that for any probability measures μ,ν\mu,\nu supported in 𝒴\mathcal{Y},

‖ϕμ−ϕν‖L2​(ρ)≤Cρ,𝒴​W1​(μ,ν)12​(1+|log⁡(W1​(μ,ν))|)12\|\phi_{\mu}-\phi_{\nu}\|_{L^{2}(\rho)}\leq C_{\rho,\mathcal{Y}}W_{1}(\mu,\nu)^{\frac{1}{2}}(1+\left|\log(W_{1}(\mu,\nu))\right|)^{\frac{1}{2}} (1.6)

If additionally D2​U≤κ′⋅IdD^{2}U\leq\kappa^{\prime}\cdot{\rm Id} then there exists Cρ,𝒴>0C_{\rho,\mathcal{Y}}>0 such that for any probability measures μ,ν\mu,\nu supported in 𝒴\mathcal{Y},

‖Tμ−Tν‖L2​(ρ)≤Cρ,𝒴​W1​(μ,ν)κ2​κ′+7​κ.\|T_{\mu}-T_{\nu}\|_{L^{2}(\rho)}\leq C_{\rho,\mathcal{Y}}W_{1}(\mu,\nu)^{\frac{\kappa}{2\kappa^{\prime}+7\kappa}}. (1.7)

To our knowledge, Theorem 1.4 is the first result establishing stability estimates for probability densities with unbounded support in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} (see for instance [48] where this is mentioned as an open problem in Section 1.4, and where the case of log-concave measures with bounded support is handled). The inequality (1.6) is sharp, up to the log factor, see Proposition 6.10. Of course, the log-loss in (1.6) may be replaced by W1​(μ,ν)−εW_{1}(\mu,\nu)^{-\varepsilon} for arbitrarily small ε>0\varepsilon>0, at the price of introducing a dependence of Cρ,𝒴C_{\rho,\mathcal{Y}} in ε\varepsilon. Also, the exponent κ2​κ′+7​κ\frac{\kappa}{2\kappa^{\prime}+7\kappa} in (1.7) can be replaced by κ2​κ′+6​κ−ε\frac{\kappa}{2\kappa^{\prime}+6\kappa}-\varepsilon for any ε>0\varepsilon>0; and again, this introduces a dependence of the constant Cρ,𝒴C_{\rho,\mathcal{Y}} in ε\varepsilon. The constants in Theorem 1.4, as well as in all other results of this paper, can be made explicit.

Remark 1.5.

Theorem 1.4, as well as the results that we describe below, are stated only for target measures which are supported in a compact set 𝒴\mathcal{Y}. This choice is mainly made for simplicity and to keep the paper readable, since handling unbounded targets would create an additional layer of complexity in the proofs. We refer to [25, Section 4] where this extension is done for ρ\rho satisfying the assumptions of Theorem 1.2.

1.2. The case of John domains

Our second result extends Theorem 1.2 to the case where ρ\rho is a probability density on a John domain, whose density is assumed to be bounded above and below by positive constants. Roughly speaking, a domain is a John domain if it is possible to move from one point to another without passing too close to the boundary. This notion is encountered for instance when dealing with Sobolev-Poincaré inequalities. Let us recall the precise definition and then provide examples.

Definition 1.6.

A bounded domain 𝒳⊂ℝd\mathcal{X}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} is called a John domain if for some point x0∈𝒳x_{0}\in\mathcal{X}, some α>0\alpha>0, and for any x∈𝒳x\in\mathcal{X}, there exists a curve γ:[0,ℓ]→𝒳\gamma:[0,\ell]\rightarrow\mathcal{X} parametrized by arc-length such that γ⁡(0)=x\gamma(0)=x, γ⁡(ℓ)=x0\gamma(\ell)=x_{0}, and

∀t∈[0,ℓ],dist⁡(γ⁡(t),∂𝒳)≥α​t\forall t\in[0,\ell],\quad{\rm dist}(\gamma(t),\partial\mathcal{X})\geq\alpha t (1.8)

where dist{\rm dist} denotes the Euclidean distance.

John domains were introduced in [39], and the terminology was coined in [44]. Lipschitz domains, and more generally domains satisfying the cone condition, are John domains. John domains may have fractal (and nonrectifiable) boundaries or internal cusps, but external cusps are excluded. The snowflake domains, domains bounded by a Koch curve and bounded quasidiscs of two­dimensional quasiconformal theory are John domains. We refer to [50] and [52, Chapter 5] for accounts on John domains.

The main result of this section is the following:

Theorem 1.7.

Let 𝒳⊂ℝd\mathcal{X}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} be a John domain and let ρ\rho be a probability density on 𝒳\mathcal{X}, bounded from above and below by positive constants. Then, for any compact set 𝒴\mathcal{Y}, there exists Cρ,𝒴>0C_{\rho,\mathcal{Y}}>0 such that for any probability measures μ,ν\mu,\nu supported in 𝒴\mathcal{Y},

‖ϕμ−ϕν‖L2​(ρ)≤Cρ,𝒴​W1​(μ,ν)12.\|\phi_{\mu}-\phi_{\nu}\|_{L^{2}(\rho)}\leq C_{\rho,\mathcal{Y}}W_{1}(\mu,\nu)^{\frac{1}{2}}. (1.9)

If in addition 𝒳\mathcal{X} has a rectifiable boundary with finite (d−1)(d-1)-dimensional Hausdorff measure, then

‖Tμ−Tν‖L2​(ρ)≤Cρ,𝒴​W1​(μ,ν)16.\|T_{\mu}-T_{\nu}\|_{L^{2}(\rho)}\leq C_{\rho,\mathcal{Y}}W_{1}(\mu,\nu)^{\frac{1}{6}}. (1.10)

The constants Cρ,𝒴C_{\rho,\mathcal{Y}} may be computed explicitly, see Lemma 3.3 and Remark 4.3 for an illustration. In Section 4.3 we show that (1.10) still holds if 𝒳\mathcal{X} is a finite union of disjoint John domains with rectifiable boundary.

Proving a converse to Theorem 1.7 is a subtle problem; we shall not attempt here to give a general characterization of the probability densities ρ\rho on compact domains for which an inequality like (1.9) (or (1.10)) holds. Nevertheless, to illustrate the relevance of the “John-type” condition in Theorem 1.7, we show that in typical examples of non-John domains considered in the literature, the stability of Brenier potentials (1.9) fails.

Definition 1.8.

We say that an absolutely continuous probability measure ρ\rho on ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} has the Hölder potential stability property if there exist C,q>0C,q>0 and p∈[1,∞)p\in[1,\infty) such that for any μ,ν\mu,\nu supported in the unit ball of ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d},

‖ϕμ−ϕν‖L2​(ρ)≤C​Wp​(μ,ν)q.\|\phi_{\mu}-\phi_{\nu}\|_{L^{2}(\rho)}\leq CW_{p}(\mu,\nu)^{q}.
Theorem 1.9.

For any d≥2d\geq 2, there exists a non-empty, bounded and path-connected domain 𝒳⊂ℝd\mathcal{X}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} such that any probability density ρ\rho which is bounded from above and below by positive constants on 𝒳\mathcal{X} does not have the Hölder potential stability property.

At least two kinds of non-John domains 𝒳\mathcal{X} can be used to prove Theorem 1.9, and they are probably the most classical examples of non-John domains. The proof we provide is based on the construction of a “room-and-passage” domain 𝒳\mathcal{X}, a class of bounded domains with thin necks at all scales already used in the literature to provide counterexamples to various spectral and functional properties known to hold in John domains (see [2], [23, pp. 521-523] for instance). In Remark 5.2 we explain that domains 𝒳\mathcal{X} with outward cusps may also be used to prove Theorem 1.9.

1.3. The case of degenerating densities in bounded domains

Theorem 1.7 shows that the convexity assumption in Theorem 1.2 may be dramatically relaxed. Our next statements demonstrate that the assumption that the probability density ρ\rho is bounded above and below on its support is not necessary either: we may allow ρ\rho to decay to 00 or blow-up to +∞+\infty at some controlled rate when approaching the boundary of 𝒳\mathcal{X}, and still obtain comparable stability bounds.

Our first result in this direction is the following. This result is new even for convex 𝒳\mathcal{X}.

Theorem 1.10.

Let ρ\rho be a probability density over a bounded Lipschitz domain 𝒳⊂ℝd\mathcal{X}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d}. Assume that there exist c1,c2>0c_{1},c_{2}>0 and δ>−1\delta>-1 such that for any x∈𝒳x\in\mathcal{X},

c1​dist​(x,∂𝒳)δ≤ρ⁡(x)≤c2​dist​(x,∂𝒳)δ.c_{1}{\rm dist}(x,\partial\mathcal{X})^{\delta}\leq\rho(x)\leq c_{2}{\rm dist}(x,\partial\mathcal{X})^{\delta}. (1.11)

Let 𝒴⊂ℝd\mathcal{Y}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} be a compact set. Then there exists Cρ,𝒴>0C_{\rho,\mathcal{Y}}>0 such that for any probability measures μ,ν\mu,\nu supported in 𝒴\mathcal{Y},

‖ϕμ−ϕν‖L2​(ρ)\displaystyle\|\phi_{\mu}-\phi_{\nu}\|_{L^{2}(\rho)} ≤Cρ,𝒴​W1​(μ,ν)12\displaystyle\leq C_{\rho,\mathcal{Y}}W_{1}(\mu,\nu)^{\frac{1}{2}} (1.12)
‖Tμ−Tν‖L2​(ρ)\displaystyle\|T_{\mu}-T_{\nu}\|_{L^{2}(\rho)} ≤Cρ,𝒴​W1​(μ,ν)16−δ′\displaystyle\leq C_{\rho,\mathcal{Y}}W_{1}(\mu,\nu)^{\frac{1}{6}-\delta^{\prime}} (1.13)

where δ′=|δ|6\delta^{\prime}=\frac{|\delta|}{6} if −1<δ≤0-1<\delta\leq 0, and δ′=δ12​(1+δ)\delta^{\prime}=\frac{\delta}{12(1+\delta)} if δ≥0\delta\geq 0.

The above condition δ>−1\delta>-1 is necessary since ρ\rho is a probability measure. In contrast with Theorem 1.10, the stability of optimal transport maps can be totally lost if the blow-up of the density ρ\rho is too strong: we exhibit in [42] an unbounded density ρ\rho on the unit ball of ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} such that for any C,q>0C,q>0, any p≥1p\geq 1 and any bounded set 𝒴⊂ℝd\mathcal{Y}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d}, the bound

∀μ,ν∈𝒫⁡(𝒴),‖Tμ−Tν‖L2​(ρ)≤C​Wp​(μ,ν)q\forall\mu,\nu\in\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Y}),\qquad\|T_{\mu}-T_{\nu}\|_{L^{2}(\rho)}\leq CW_{p}(\mu,\nu)^{q}

fails.

Our second result concerning densities degenerating at the boundary of a bounded domain is motivated by works in statistics (starting with [20]) which define notions of multivariate quantiles and statistical depth via optimal transport theory. These works aim at addressing the well-known problem of finding a good analogue in dimension d≥2d\geq 2 of univariate distribution functions, despite the absence of a canonical ordering relation in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}. Compared to previous notions considered in the literature, the notion introduced in [20] and further studied e.g. in [36], [31], enjoys inferential properties expected from distribution and quantile functions in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}. Given a probability density μ\mu, the vector quantile map defined in [20] is the quadratic optimal transport map from the spherical uniform distribution ρ\rho defined in Theorem 1.11 to μ\mu: the quantiles of μ\mu are defined by pushing forward the quantiles of ρ\rho. The main theoretical result of [20], namely [20, Theorem 3.1], establishes that for any compactly supported probability density μ\mu, the empirical vector quantile maps defined via empirical approximations of μ\mu converge to the vector quantile map associated to μ\mu (actually, [20, Theorem 3.1] shows that convergence holds even if ρ\rho itself is replaced by empirical approximations). Our next statement, when applied to an empirical approximation ν\nu of μ\mu, quantifies the rate of convergence:

Theorem 1.11.

Let 𝒳=B⁡(0,1)∖{0}\mathcal{X}=B(0,1)\setminus\{0\} where B⁡(0,1)B(0,1) is the closed unit ball of ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}. Consider the probability density ρ⁡(x)=cd​|x|1−d​χ𝒳​(x)\rho(x)=c_{d}|x|^{1-d}\chi_{\mathcal{X}}(x) where χ𝒳\chi_{\mathcal{X}} is the characteristic function of 𝒳\mathcal{X} and cdc_{d} is a normalizing constant. Let 𝒴⊂ℝd\mathcal{Y}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} be a compact set. Then there exists Cd,𝒴>0C_{d,\mathcal{Y}}>0 such that for any probability measures μ,ν\mu,\nu supported in 𝒴\mathcal{Y},

‖ϕμ−ϕν‖L2​(ρ)\displaystyle\|\phi_{\mu}-\phi_{\nu}\|_{L^{2}(\rho)} ≤Cd,𝒴​W1​(μ,ν)12\displaystyle\leq C_{d,\mathcal{Y}}W_{1}(\mu,\nu)^{\frac{1}{2}} (1.14)
‖Tμ−Tν‖L2​(ρ)\displaystyle\|T_{\mu}-T_{\nu}\|_{L^{2}(\rho)} ≤Cd,𝒴​W1​(μ,ν)16​d.\displaystyle\leq C_{d,\mathcal{Y}}W_{1}(\mu,\nu)^{\frac{1}{6d}}. (1.15)

The exponent in the upper bound (1.15) depends on dd, and we do not know if it possible to get rid of this dependence. We explain in Remark 4.8 that our proof techniques could potentially handle other families of probability measures ρ\rho whose density tends to 00 or +∞+\infty than those considered in Theorems 1.10 and 1.11. We chose the above statements for their simplicity and their relevance regarding applications.

1.4. Generalized Cauchy distributions

We finally establish stability estimates for Brenier potentials and Brenier maps in the case where ρ\rho belongs to a family of probability measures on ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} which are not log-concave. Namely, we handle generalized Cauchy distributions of the form ρ⁡(x)=c⁡(x)​⟨x⟩−β\rho(x)=c(x)\langle x\rangle^{-\beta} where here and in the sequel

⟨x⟩=(1+|x|2)1/2.\langle x\rangle=(1+|x|^{2})^{1/2}.

From now on, we assume that β>d+2\beta>d+2. This ensures that ρ\rho has finite second moment, and is in particular necessary for the left-hand side of (1.16) to be finite.

Theorem 1.12.

Assume that ρ⁡(x)=c⁡(x)​⟨x⟩−β\rho(x)=c(x)\langle x\rangle^{-\beta} on ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}, with β>d+2\beta>d+2 and 0<m≤c⁡(x)≤M<+∞0<m\leq c(x)\leq M<+\infty. Let 𝒴⊂ℝd\mathcal{Y}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} be a compact set. Then, there exists Cρ,𝒴>0C_{\rho,\mathcal{Y}}>0 such that for any probability measures μ,ν\mu,\nu supported in 𝒴\mathcal{Y},

‖ϕμ−ϕν‖L2​(ρ)\displaystyle\|\phi_{\mu}-\phi_{\nu}\|_{L^{2}(\rho)} ≤Cρ,𝒴​W1​(μ,ν)θ\displaystyle\leq C_{\rho,\mathcal{Y}}W_{1}(\mu,\nu)^{\theta} (1.16)
‖Tμ−Tν‖L2​(ρ)\displaystyle\|T_{\mu}-T_{\nu}\|_{L^{2}(\rho)} ≤Cρ,𝒴​W1​(μ,ν)θ′\displaystyle\leq C_{\rho,\mathcal{Y}}W_{1}(\mu,\nu)^{\theta^{\prime}} (1.17)

where θ=12​(1−2β−d)>0\theta=\frac{1}{2}(1-\frac{2}{\beta-d})>0 and θ′=β−d−28​β−2​d−4>0\theta^{\prime}=\frac{\beta-d-2}{8\beta-2d-4}>0. Moreover, the exponent θ=12​(1−2β−d)\theta=\frac{1}{2}(1-\frac{2}{\beta-d}) in (1.16) is sharp.

With this result, we want in particular to challenge a natural idea that could arise from our results of the previous sections and their proofs, namely that there could exist a strict equivalence between stability estimates for Brenier potentials with source measure ρ\rho and the fact that the Poincaré(-Wirtinger) inequality holds for ρ\rho. But Theorem 1.12 disproves this conjectural relation, since it is known that the Poincaré inequality does not hold for generalized Cauchy distributions, see e.g. [8]. However, this does not rule out the possibility of a weaker relationship between the two properties: as emphasized in Section 6.6, generalized Cauchy distributions satisfy a weighted Poincaré inequality, which may be recovered as a direct corollary of our proof.

One more motivation for Theorem 1.12 is that its proof requires to develop a different strategy compared to our other results, and we believe this strategy to be of independent interest. See Sections 1.5 and 6.1 for details. This strategy may be used for instance to reprove weaker versions of Theorems 1.4 and 1.7; we shall not pursue this here. Refining this strategy, it is possible to prove analogous stability estimates for Brenier potentials and Brenier maps for other families of source measures which do not satisfy a Poincaré inequality, for instance ρ⁡(x)=c⁡(x)​e−κ​|x|α\rho(x)=c(x)e^{-\kappa|x|^{\alpha}} with 0<α<10<\alpha<1, κ>0\kappa>0, and 0<m≤c⁡(x)≤M<+∞0<m\leq c(x)\leq M<+\infty. We do not pursue this here either, we only give a few more details in Remark 6.11.

1.5. Proof strategies and organization of the paper

The starting point of our proofs is to reinterpret the quantity ‖ϕμ−ϕν‖L2​(ρ)2\|\phi_{\mu}-\phi_{\nu}\|^{2}_{L^{2}(\rho)} as a variance Varρ​(ϕμ−ϕν){\rm Var}_{\rho}(\phi_{\mu}-\phi_{\nu}), due to the fact that both ϕμ\phi_{\mu} and ϕν\phi_{\nu} have vanishing mean with respect to ρ\rho. In Section 2.1 we establish a variance inequality, i.e., an upper bound on this variance, in the case where ρ\rho is supported in a compact convex set and bounded above and below by positive constants. This variance inequality is a refinement of the results of [25]. We provide a proof which simplifies the approach of [25]. In Section 2.2 we deduce Theorem 1.4 via truncation arguments.

To prove the other results we follow a strategy which could as well be used to prove Poincaré-Wirtinger inequalities of the form Varρ​(f)≤C​∫|∇f|2​𝑑ρ{\rm Var}_{\rho}(f)\leq C\int|\nabla f|^{2}d\rho where here and in the sequel

Varρ​(f)=infc∈ℝ∫ℝd|f−c|2​𝑑ρ.{\rm Var}_{\rho}(f)=\inf_{c\in\mathbb{R}}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}|f-c|^{2}d\rho.

Namely, we rely on two ingredients: firstly, the upper bound on the variance in convex sets established in Section 2.1; secondly, an argument to glue together “local” variance inequalities in small convex sets and deduce an upper bound on the “global” variance, i.e., the variance in 𝒳\mathcal{X}.

Our main contribution is related to the second ingredient: we extend already existing techniques and develop new methods to glue together “local” variance inequalities. Overall, the leitmotiv of this work is that if a function ff does not vary much in each set QQ of a family ℱ\mathcal{F}, and if these sets intersect enough, then ff does not vary much in the union of the sets Q∈ℱQ\in\mathcal{F}. To turn this rough idea into proofs, we use domain decompositions techniques which we describe below. Let us already mention that once the global variance inequality is proved, we deduce almost immediately the stability estimates on the difference of Brenier potentials ‖ϕμ−ϕν‖L2​(ρ)\|\phi_{\mu}-\phi_{\nu}\|_{L^{2}(\rho)} via Kantorovich-Rubinstein duality. The stability of Brenier maps requires more work, it essentially relies on reverse Poincaré inequalities for the difference of two convex functions proved in [25] (i.e., ‖∇ϕμ−∇ϕν‖L2≤C​‖ϕμ−ϕν‖L2θ\|\nabla\phi_{\mu}-\nabla\phi_{\nu}\|_{L^{2}}\leq C\|\phi_{\mu}-\phi_{\nu}\|_{L^{2}}^{\theta}).

A key point is thus to understand how to glue together variance inequalities. For this, we develop two strategies, which are compared in Section 6.7.

Our first method is set out in Section 3, see notably Theorem 3.6. To prove a global variance inequality, we take inspiration from the proof of Sobolev-Poincaré inequalities in John domains ([9], [35]): we rely on the Whitney decomposition and its good properties in John domains, in particular the existence of a decomposition satisfying a Boman chain condition in the spirit of [10], [9]. In Section 4 we use this to prove Theorems 1.7, 1.10 and 1.11, which requires in each case to establish some doubling property for the probability measure ρ\rho. The counterexample to Hölder potential stability in non-John domains used to prove Theorem 1.9 is provided in Section 5. As already mentioned, it is based on the construction of an appropriate “room-and-passage” domain.

Our second method for gluing variance inequalities is developed in Section 6 and allows us to prove Theorem 1.12. It consists in decomposing 𝒳\mathcal{X} into convex sets and constructing a weighted combinatorial graph from this decomposition, with one vertex for each convex set and one edge for each pair of overlapping convex sets. To be able to control the variance in 𝒳\mathcal{X} by the variances in the convex sets we need enough overlap between these sets, in other words that the weighted graph is sufficiently well connected. This connectedness is measured via the spectral gap of the graph Laplacian, which we prove to be strictly positive via a Cheeger inequality proved in Appendix B.

Apart from the families of ρ\rho’s handled in Section 1.4, all the ρ\rho’s considered in the present work support an L2L^{2}-Poincaré-Wirtinger inequality. These Poincaré-Wirtinger inequalities are actually immediate corollaries of the techniques of this paper, see e.g. Section 3.3. It might seem natural to conjecture that if ρ\rho supports a Poincaré(-Wirtinger) inequality, then not only the Brenier potentials are unique (which is a consequence of connectedness of the support, see Section 3.3), but they are even stable. However, this is totally unclear at the present moment, and we know by Theorem 1.12 that the converse is false.

Finally, we believe that the techniques of the present paper, which show that it is sufficient to establish local variance inequalities in order to prove global stability results, might foster progress in other directions, for instance regarding the stability of optimal transport maps for more general costs (and on Riemannian manifolds), the random matching problem and rates of convergence for the Sinkhorn algorithm.

1.6. Notation

Throughout the paper, ℕ\mathbb{N} denotes the set of non-negative integers. For any nn in the set of positive integers ℕ∗\mathbb{N}^{*}, the notation [n][n] stands for [n]={1,…,n}[n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}. The characteristic function of a set S⊂ℝdS\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} is denoted by χS\chi_{S}. The Euclidean distance in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} is denoted by dist{\rm dist}. The Euclidean scalar product is denoted by ⟨⋅|⋅⟩\langle\cdot|\cdot\rangle, and this notation also stands for the duality pairing between continuous functions with compact support and real-valued Radon measures (the distinction between the two is clear from the context). The Euclidean (closed) ball of center 00 and radius r≥0r\geq 0 is denoted by ℬr:=B⁡(0,r)\mathcal{B}_{r}:=B(0,r). The Lebesgue measure on ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} is denoted by λ\lambda. The support of a measure ρ\rho is denoted by spt⁡(ρ){\rm spt}(\rho). Absolutely continuous measures on ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} are sometimes identified with their density with respect to the Lebesgue measure.

2. Stability for log-concave sources

2.1. Variance inequality in compact convex sets

In this section, we start with the case where ρ\rho is supported on a compact and convex set. We establish a variance inequality which is a key ingredient for most of the proofs in the present work.

Given a function ψ:ℝd→ℝ∪{+∞},\psi:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}, we recall that its convex conjugate is defined as

ψ∗​(x)=supy∈ℝd⟨x|y⟩−ψ⁡(y)\psi^{*}(x)=\sup_{y\in\mathbb{R}^{d}}\ \langle x|y\rangle-\psi(y) (2.1)

If ψ∈𝒞0​(𝒴)\psi\in\mathcal{C}^{0}(\mathcal{Y}) where 𝒴⊂ℝd\mathcal{Y}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} (thus ψ\psi is a priori not defined on ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}), we implicitly extend ψ\psi by +∞+\infty outside of 𝒴\mathcal{Y} when computing ψ∗\psi^{*}. This is equivalent to taking the supremum in (2.1) over y∈𝒴y\in\mathcal{Y}.

The following statement is a minor modification of [25], [48]. Due to its importance in what follows, we provide here a complete proof.

Theorem 2.1.

Let Q⊂ℝdQ\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} be a compact convex set with non-empty interior, let σ\sigma be a logarithmically-concave probability density over QQ and let ρ\rho be another probability density over QQ satisfying mρ​σ≤ρ≤Mρ​σm_{\rho}\sigma\leq\rho\leq M_{\rho}\sigma for some constants Mρ≥mρ>0M_{\rho}\geq m_{\rho}>0. Let 𝒴⊂ℝd\mathcal{Y}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} be a compact set and set R𝒴=maxy∈𝒴⁡‖y‖R_{\mathcal{Y}}=\max_{y\in\mathcal{Y}}\|y\|. Then, for all ψ0,ψ1∈𝒞0​(𝒴),\psi_{0},\psi_{1}\in\mathcal{C}^{0}(\mathcal{Y}),

⟨ψ1−ψ0|∇ψ0​#∗ρ−∇ψ1​#∗ρ⟩≥e−1mρMρ1R𝒴​diam​(Q)Varρ(ψ1∗−ψ0∗).\langle\psi_{1}-\psi_{0}|\nabla\psi_{0\#}^{*}\rho-\nabla\psi_{1\#}^{*}\rho\rangle\geq e^{-1}\frac{m_{\rho}}{M_{\rho}}\frac{1}{R_{\mathcal{Y}}{\rm diam}(Q)}{\rm Var}_{\rho}(\psi_{1}^{*}-\psi_{0}^{*}). (2.2)

An example to keep in mind is when σ\sigma is the characteristic function of QQ, normalized to be a probability density. Another important example is when ρ\rho itself is log-concave, in which case we may take σ=ρ\sigma=\rho and mρ/Mρ=1m_{\rho}/M_{\rho}=1.

Before giving the proof of Theorem 2.1 we recall the following result from [25], which we shall use several times in this work.

Proposition 2.2.

[25, Proposition 4.1] Let KK be a compact domain of ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} with rectifiable boundary and let u,v:K→ℝu,v:K\rightarrow\mathbb{R} be two LL-Lipschitz functions on KK that are convex on any segment included in KK. Then there exists a constant CdC_{d} depending only on dd such that

‖∇u−∇v‖L2​(λ,K)2≤Cd​ℋd−1​(∂K)2/3​L4/3​‖u−v‖L2​(λ,K)2/3\|\nabla u-\nabla v\|_{L^{2}(\lambda,K)}^{2}\leq C_{d}\mathcal{H}^{d-1}(\partial K)^{2/3}L^{4/3}\|u-v\|_{L^{2}(\lambda,K)}^{2/3} (2.3)

where ℋd−1\mathcal{H}^{d-1} denotes the (d−1)(d-1)-dimensional Hausdorff measure and the norms in (2.3) are taken with respect to the dd-dimensional Lebesgue measure λ\lambda.

We turn to the proof of Theorem 2.1.

Proof of Theorem 2.1.

As in [25], the proof mainly consists in proving a strong convexity property for the Kantorovich functional 𝒦ρ:𝒞0​(𝒴)→ℝ\mathcal{K}_{\rho}:\mathcal{C}^{0}(\mathcal{Y})\rightarrow\mathbb{R},

𝒦ρ​(ψ)=∫Qψ∗​𝑑ρ.\mathcal{K}_{\rho}(\psi)=\int_{Q}\psi^{*}d\rho.

Step 1: Restriction to QQ-convex functions. In the following, we fix a closed ball BB containing QQ in its interior. A function ψ:ℝd→ℝ\psi:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R} is called QQ-convex if it is equal to the convex conjugate of a convex and Lipschitz function ϕ\phi defined on BB, i.e. ψ⁡(y)=maxx∈B⁡⟨x|y⟩−ϕ⁡(x)\psi(y)=\max_{x\in B}\langle x|y\rangle-\phi(x). In this case, Fenchel-Rockafellar’s theorem implies that ϕ=ψ∗\phi=\psi^{*} on BB. Note that if ψ∈𝒞0​(𝒴)\psi\in\mathcal{C}^{0}(\mathcal{Y}), then

ψ^​(y)=(ψ∗|B)∗​(y)=maxx∈B⁡⟨x|y⟩−ψ∗​(x)\hat{\psi}(y)=\left(\left.\psi^{*}\right|_{B}\right)^{*}(y)=\max_{x\in B}\langle x|y\rangle-\psi^{*}(x) (2.4)

Our first step is to prove that the inequality (2.2) for any pair of QQ-convex functions implies the same inequality for any pair of continuous functions on 𝒴\mathcal{Y}. To do so, we consider ψ0,ψ1∈𝒞0​(𝒴)\psi_{0},\psi_{1}\in\mathcal{C}^{0}(\mathcal{Y}) and we define ψ^0\hat{\psi}_{0} and ψ^1\hat{\psi}_{1} as in (2.4). Since the convex functions ψ^i∗\hat{\psi}_{i}^{*} and ψi∗\psi_{i}^{*} agree on QQ, the right-hand side of the inequality (2.2) is unchanged under the transformation ψi→ψ^i\psi_{i}\to\hat{\psi}_{i}:

3. Variance inequalities

Our proofs of Theorems 1.7, 1.10 and 1.11 mainly rely on a variance inequality for the dual potentials (Theorem 3.6), which extends Theorem 2.1 to all probability densities ρ\rho having the following three properties: (i) the support of ρ\rho can be decomposed into a family ℱ\mathcal{F} of cubes satisfying the so-called Boman chain condition (see Definition 3.2); (ii) a doubling property (3.7); (iii) a uniform upper bound (3.18) on the maximum and minimum value of ρ\rho in each cube of this decomposition.

In Section 3.1, we provide reminders on the Whitney decomposition and the Boman chain condition. Then in Section 3.2 we prove a lemma showing how to glue variance inequalities together when items (i) and (ii) described above hold. The proof of this lemma relies on techniques developed to prove Poincaré-Sobolev inequalities in John domains (see for instance [9]). Finally in Section 3.4 we deduce the variance inequality (Theorem 3.6).

3.1. Whitney decomposition and the Boman chain condition

Let us first recall briefly the Whitney decomposition (see [34, Appendix J.1] for a proof). A dyadic cube in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} is a cube of the form

{(x1,…,xd)∈ℝd∣mj​2−ℓ≤xj<(mj+1)​2−ℓ​for any ​j∈[d]}\left\{(x_{1},\ldots,x_{d})\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\mid m_{j}2^{-\ell}\leq x_{j}<(m_{j}+1)2^{-\ell}\ \text{for any }j\in[d]\right\}

where ℓ∈ℤ\ell\in\mathbb{Z} and mj∈ℤm_{j}\in\mathbb{Z} for any j∈[d]j\in[d]. Roughly speaking, the Whitney decomposition is a decomposition of any open set into dyadic cubes in a way that each of these cubes has a sidelength which is comparable to its distance from the boundary of the open set.

Lemma 3.1 (Whitney decomposition).

Let 𝒳\mathcal{X} be an open non-empty proper subset of ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}. Then there exists a family of closed dyadic cubes PjP_{j} such that

  • •

    The PjP_{j}’s have disjoint interiors and

    ⋃jPj=𝒳.\bigcup_{j}P_{j}=\mathcal{X}.
  • •

    If ℓ⁡(P)\ell(P) denotes the sidelength of a cube PP and 𝒳c=ℝd∖𝒳\mathcal{X}^{c}=\mathbb{R}^{d}\setminus\mathcal{X},

    d​ℓ​(Pj)≤dist⁡(Pj,𝒳c)≤4​d​ℓ​(Pj).{\sqrt{d}}\ell(P_{j})\leq{\rm dist}(P_{j},\mathcal{X}^{c})\leq 4{\sqrt{d}}\ell(P_{j}). (3.1)
  • •

    If the boundaries of two cubes PjP_{j} and PkP_{k} touch then

    14≤ℓ⁡(Pj)ℓ⁡(Pk)≤4.{\frac{1}{4}}\leq{\frac{\ell(P_{j})}{\ell(P_{k})}}\leq 4. (3.2)
  • •

    For a given PjP_{j} there exist at most 12d12^{d} cubes PkP_{k}’s that touch it.

  • •

    Let 1<σ<5/41<\sigma<5/4. If QjQ_{j} denotes the cube with same center as PjP_{j} and ℓ⁡(Qj)=σ​ℓ​(Pj)\ell(Q_{j})=\sigma\ell(P_{j}), then

    ∑jχQj≤12d\sum_{j}\chi_{Q_{j}}\leq 12^{d}

    where χQj\chi_{Q_{j}} is the characteristic function of QjQ_{j}.

Under some assumptions on 𝒳\mathcal{X} and ρ\rho that are studied in Section 4, the cubes QjQ_{j} of the last item of the above lemma (for some fixed σ∈(1,5/4)\sigma\in(1,5/4)) provide another decomposition of 𝒳\mathcal{X} into cubes which now overlap, and which satisfy the properties listed below ([10, Lemma 2.1], [9, Section 3], [38, Section 4]):

Definition 3.2 (Boman chain condition).

Let σ≥1\sigma\geq 1 and A,B,C>1A,B,C>1. A probability measure ρ\rho on an open set 𝒳⊂ℝd\mathcal{X}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} satisfies the Boman chain condition with parameters A,B,CA,B,C if there exists a covering ℱ\mathcal{F} of 𝒳\mathcal{X} by open cubes Q∈ℱQ\in\mathcal{F} such that

  • •

    for σ=min⁡(10/9,(d+1)/d)\sigma=\min(10/9,(d+1)/d) and for any x∈ℝdx\in\mathbb{R}^{d},

    ∑Q∈ℱχσ​Q​(x)≤A​χ𝒳​(x).\sum_{Q\in\mathcal{F}}\chi_{\sigma Q}(x)\leq A\chi_{\mathcal{X}}(x). (3.3)
  • •

    For some fixed cube Q0Q_{0} in ℱ\mathcal{F}, called the central cube, and for every Q∈ℱQ\in\mathcal{F}, there exists a chain Q0,Q1,…,QN=QQ_{0},Q_{1},\ldots,Q_{N}=Q of distinct cubes from ℱ\mathcal{F} such that for any j∈{0,…,N−1}j\in\{0,\ldots,N-1\},

    Q⊂B​QjQ\subset BQ_{j} (3.4)

    where B​QjBQ_{j} is the cube with same center as QjQ_{j}, and sidelength multiplied by BB.

  • •

    Consecutive cubes of the above chain overlap quantitatively: for any j∈{0,…,N−1}j\in\{0,\ldots,N-1\},

    ρ⁡(Qj∩Qj+1)≥C−1​max⁡(ρ⁡(Qj),ρ⁡(Qj+1)).\rho(Q_{j}\cap Q_{j+1})\geq C^{-1}\max(\rho(Q_{j}),\rho(Q_{j+1})). (3.5)

Note that in the above definition, the length NN of the connecting chain depends on Q∈ℱQ\in\mathcal{F} and is not assumed to be uniformly bounded in Q∈ℱQ\in\mathcal{F}. Also we could have replaced σ​Q\sigma Q in (3.3) simply by QQ for the purpose of this paper, but we keep the same convention as in [10], [9], [38] to remain coherent with the literature. Finally, let us observe that (3.5) implies that consecutive cubes of the above chain are comparable in size: for any j∈{0,…,N−1}j\in\{0,\ldots,N-1\},

C−1≤ρ⁡(Qj)ρ⁡(Qj+1)≤C.C^{-1}\leq\frac{\rho(Q_{j})}{\rho(Q_{j+1})}\leq C. (3.6)

Indeed, if (3.5) holds, then

ρ⁡(Qj)≥ρ⁡(Qj∩Qj+1)≥C−1​max⁡(ρ⁡(Qj),ρ⁡(Qj+1))≥C−1​ρ​(Qj+1),\rho(Q_{j})\geq\rho(Q_{j}\cap Q_{j+1})\geq C^{-1}\max(\rho(Q_{j}),\rho(Q_{j+1}))\geq C^{-1}\rho(Q_{j+1}),

and the other bound in (3.6) is proved in the same way by reversing jj and j+1j+1.

3.3. Remarks on uniqueness of Brenier potentials and Poincaré-Wirtinger inequalities

Before stating and proving the main result of Section 3, namely Theorem 3.6, let us comment on uniqueness of Brenier potentials and link Lemma 3.3 with Poincaré-Wirtinger inequalities. In the settings considered in the present paper, Brenier potentials are always unique: this is a consequence of the connectedness of the support of ρ\rho, see for instance [53, Proposition 7.18] or [55, Remark 10.30]. However, if the support of ρ\rho is not connected, then in general the Brenier potentials are not unique:

Proposition 3.5.

Let 𝒳1\mathcal{X}_{1} and 𝒳2\mathcal{X}_{2} be two non-empty bounded subsets of ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} with dist⁡(𝒳1,𝒳2)>0{\rm dist}(\mathcal{X}_{1},\mathcal{X}_{2})>0. Let ρ\rho be a probability measure on 𝒳=𝒳1∪𝒳2\mathcal{X}=\mathcal{X}_{1}\cup\mathcal{X}_{2} such that min⁡(ρ⁡(𝒳1),ρ⁡(𝒳2))>0\min(\rho(\mathcal{X}_{1}),\rho(\mathcal{X}_{2}))>0. Then there exists a 11-parameter family of Brenier potentials corresponding to the identity mapping on 𝒳\mathcal{X} (which is the optimal transport map between ρ\rho and ρ\rho), and any two of them are not ρ\rho-almost everywhere equal.

Proof.

Consider ϕα​(x)=12​|x|2+α​χ𝒳1​(x)+cα\phi_{\alpha}(x)=\frac{1}{2}|x|^{2}+\alpha\chi_{\mathcal{X}_{1}}(x)+c_{\alpha}, where χ𝒳1\chi_{\mathcal{X}_{1}} is the characteristic function of 𝒳1\mathcal{X}_{1} and cαc_{\alpha} is chosen so that ∫𝒳ϕα​(x)​𝑑ρ​(x)=0\int_{\mathcal{X}}\phi_{\alpha}(x)d\rho(x)=0. Then ∇ϕα\nabla\phi_{\alpha} transports ρ\rho to itself for any α\alpha, and it is easy to check that for 0≤α<dist​(𝒳1,𝒳2)2/20\leq\alpha<{\rm dist}(\mathcal{X}_{1},\mathcal{X}_{2})^{2}/2, there holds (ϕα∗)∗=ϕα(\phi_{\alpha}^{*})^{*}=\phi_{\alpha} on 𝒳\mathcal{X}. Thus ∇ϕα\nabla\phi_{\alpha} is actually the optimal transport map. ∎

Let us point out that in the setting of Lemma 3.3, not only the support of ρ\rho is connected, but ρ\rho even satisfies an L2L^{2}-Poincaré-Wirtinger inequality. Therefore, uniqueness of Brenier potentials may be checked also in the following way: the equality ∇ϕ=∇ϕ′\nabla\phi=\nabla\phi^{\prime} ρ\rho-almost everywhere together with ∫𝒳ϕ​𝑑ρ=∫𝒳ϕ′​𝑑ρ=0\int_{\mathcal{X}}\phi d\rho=\int_{\mathcal{X}}\phi^{\prime}d\rho=0 implies that ϕ=ϕ′\phi=\phi^{\prime}. Let us show that if ρ\rho satisfies the assumptions of Lemma 3.3 and also satisfies supQMρ~Qmρ~Q<+∞\sup_{Q}\frac{M_{\tilde{\rho}_{Q}}}{m_{\tilde{\rho}_{Q}}}<+\infty, then it supports a L2L^{2}-Poincaré-Wirtinger inequality:

Varρ​(f)≤CP​∫𝒳|∇f|2​𝑑ρ.{\rm Var}_{\rho}(f)\leq C_{P}\int_{\mathcal{X}}|\nabla f|^{2}d\rho. (3.14)

To prove (3.14), we first observe that there exists CP′>0C_{P}^{\prime}>0 such that for any Q∈ℱQ\in\mathcal{F} there holds

Varρ~Q​(f)≤CP′​∫Q|∇f|2​d​ρ~Q.{\rm Var}_{\tilde{\rho}_{Q}}(f)\leq C_{P}^{\prime}\int_{Q}|\nabla f|^{2}d\tilde{\rho}_{Q}. (3.15)

Indeed, since supQMρ~Qmρ~Q<+∞\sup_{Q}\frac{M_{\tilde{\rho}_{Q}}}{m_{\tilde{\rho}_{Q}}}<+\infty, it is sufficient to prove that (3.15) holds when ρ~Q\tilde{\rho}_{Q} is replaced by the normalized Lebesgue measure on QQ, with a QQ-independent constant CP′C_{P}^{\prime}. This latter fact holds because all QQ are cubes, with uniformly bounded diameter. Summing (3.15) over Q∈ℱQ\in\mathcal{F} with weights ρ⁡(Q)\rho(Q), and using (3.3) we get (3.14).

3.4. The variance inequality

In the rest of the paper, for any probability density ρ0\rho_{0} supported on 𝒳0⊂ℝd\mathcal{X}_{0}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} we set

Given a compact set 𝒴⊂ℝd\mathcal{Y}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d}, we set

R𝒴=maxy∈𝒴⁡|y|.R_{\mathcal{Y}}=\max_{y\in\mathcal{Y}}|y|. (3.17)

Theorem 3.6.

Varρ​(ψ1∗−ψ0∗)≤C′​⟨ψ0−ψ1|(∇ψ1∗)#​ρ−(∇ψ0∗)#​ρ⟩.{\rm Var}_{\rho}\left(\psi_{1}^{*}-\psi_{0}^{*}\right)\leq C^{\prime}\langle\psi_{0}-\psi_{1}|(\nabla\psi_{1}^{*})_{\#}\rho-(\nabla\psi_{0}^{*})_{\#}\rho\rangle. (3.19)
Proof of Theorem 3.6.

Varρ~Q​(ψ1∗−ψ0∗)≤CDM​⟨ψ0−ψ1|(∇ψ1∗)#​ρ~Q−(∇ψ0∗)#​ρ~Q⟩{\rm Var}_{\tilde{\rho}_{Q}}\left(\psi_{1}^{*}-\psi_{0}^{*}\right)\leq C_{\rm DM}\langle\psi_{0}-\psi_{1}|(\nabla\psi_{1}^{*})_{\#}\tilde{\rho}_{Q}-(\nabla\psi_{0}^{*})_{\#}\tilde{\rho}_{Q}\rangle (3.20)

We define a partition ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime} of 𝒳\mathcal{X} as follows: x,x′x,x^{\prime} belong to the same element P∈ℱ′P\in\mathcal{F}^{\prime} if and only if they belong to exactly the same elements of ℱ\mathcal{F}. Hence it follows from (3.21) and the lower bound ⟨ψ0−ψ1|(∇ψ1∗)#ρ|P−(∇ψ0∗)#ρ|P⟩≥0\langle\psi_{0}-\psi_{1}|(\nabla\psi_{1}^{*})_{\#}\rho_{|P}-(\nabla\psi_{0}^{*})_{\#}\rho_{|P}\rangle\geq 0 valid for any P∈ℱ′P\in\mathcal{F}^{\prime} that

Varρ​(ψ1∗−ψ0∗)\displaystyle{\rm Var}_{\rho}(\psi_{1}^{*}-\psi_{0}^{*}) ≤200A3CD3CDM∑P∈ℱ′⟨ψ0−ψ1|(∇ψ1∗)#ρ|P−(∇ψ0∗)#ρ|P⟩\displaystyle\leq 200A^{3}CD^{3}C_{\rm DM}\sum_{P\in\mathcal{F}^{\prime}}\langle\psi_{0}-\psi_{1}|(\nabla\psi_{1}^{*})_{\#}\rho_{|P}-(\nabla\psi_{0}^{*})_{\#}\rho_{|P}\rangle (3.22)
=200​A3​C​D3​CDM​⟨ψ0−ψ1|(∇ψ1∗)#​ρ−(∇ψ0∗)#​ρ⟩\displaystyle=200A^{3}CD^{3}C_{\rm DM}\langle\psi_{0}-\psi_{1}|(\nabla\psi_{1}^{*})_{\#}\rho-(\nabla\psi_{0}^{*})_{\#}\rho\rangle (3.23)

(the last equality holds because ℱ′\mathcal{F}^{\prime} is a partition). This proves Theorem 3.6. ∎

4. Proof of Theorems 1.7, 1.10 and 1.11: bounded domains

We prove successively Theorems 1.7, 1.10 and 1.11 in Sections 4.2, 4.4 and 4.5 respectively. These three proofs are based on the variance inequality proved in Theorem 3.6. We apply it to the dual Brenier potentials: recalling that the Brenier potential associated to the optimal transport from ρ\rho to μ\mu is denoted by ϕμ\phi_{\mu} (and is extended by +∞+\infty outside 𝒳\mathcal{X}), its Legendre transform defined by

∀y∈𝒴,ψμ​(y)=supx∈𝒳⟨x|y⟩−ϕμ​(x)\forall y\in\mathcal{Y},\qquad\psi_{\mu}(y)=\sup_{x\in\mathcal{X}}\ \langle x|y\rangle-\phi_{\mu}(x) (4.1)

is called the dual Brenier potential. Since 𝒳\mathcal{X} is bounded, ψμ\psi_{\mu} is a (convex) diam⁡(𝒳){\rm diam}(\mathcal{X})-Lipschitz function on 𝒴\mathcal{Y}. Moreover, since ϕμ\phi_{\mu} is convex, ψμ∗=ϕμ\psi_{\mu}^{*}=\phi_{\mu} where ψμ∗\psi_{\mu}^{*} is defined via (2.1), or equivalently

∀x∈𝒳,ψμ∗​(x)=supy∈𝒴⟨x|y⟩−ψμ​(y).\forall x\in\mathcal{X},\qquad\psi_{\mu}^{*}(x)=\sup_{y\in\mathcal{Y}}\ \langle x|y\rangle-\psi_{\mu}(y).

We start in Section 4.1 with the construction of a family ℱ\mathcal{F} of cubes which will be used in all three proofs as the covering of the Boman chain condition.

4.1. Construction of the Boman cubes

Let 𝒳\mathcal{X} be a non-empty proper John domain of ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}, and consider its Whitney decomposition into closed dyadic cubes PjP_{j} recalled in Lemma 3.1. Let us fix σ=min⁡(10/9,(d+1)/d)\sigma=\min(10/9,(d+1)/d). For any jj, we set Qj=σ​PjQ_{j}=\sigma P_{j}; then ℱ\mathcal{F} is defined as the set of all QjQ_{j}. In particular, due to (3.1), there holds

12​d​ℓ​(Qj)≤dist⁡(Qj,𝒳c)≤5​d​ℓ​(Qj).\frac{1}{2}{\sqrt{d}}\ell(Q_{j})\leq{\rm dist}(Q_{j},\mathcal{X}^{c})\leq 5{\sqrt{d}}\ell(Q_{j}). (4.2)

In the next sections, we will use this decomposition (Qj)j∈ℱ(Q_{j})_{j\in\mathcal{F}} to verify the Boman chain condition. Of course, condition (3.5) depends on the density ρ\rho that we put on 𝒳\mathcal{X}; but it is already possible to verify (3.3) and (3.4), which are properties of ℱ\mathcal{F} (and 𝒳\mathcal{X}), independent of ρ\rho.

Let us first check (3.3). Denote by 𝒲\mathcal{W} the set of cubes in the Whitney decomposition of 𝒳\mathcal{X}. For x∈𝒳x\in\mathcal{X},

∑Qj∈ℱχσ​Qj​(x)=∑Pj∈𝒲χσ2​Pj​(x)≤12d\sum_{Q_{j}\in\mathcal{F}}\chi_{\sigma Q_{j}}(x)=\sum_{P_{j}\in\mathcal{W}}\chi_{\sigma^{2}P_{j}}(x)\leq 12^{d}

where we used σ2<5/4\sigma^{2}<5/4 and the last property of the Whitney decomposition listed in Lemma 3.1. For x∉𝒳x\notin\mathcal{X}, notice that xx does not belong to any cube σ​Qj\sigma Q_{j} due to (4.2), and therefore (3.3) also holds in this case. Then, (3.4) is a consequence of 𝒳\mathcal{X} being a John domain, according to the following result:

Lemma 4.1.

(see [10, Lemma 2.1]) Let 𝒳⊂ℝd\mathcal{X}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} be a John domain, and let mm denote the Lebesgue measure on 𝒳\mathcal{X}. Then mm satisfies the Boman chain condition for the above covering (Qj)j∈ℱ(Q_{j})_{j\in\mathcal{F}} and some A,B,C>0A,B,C>0. In particular, (3.4) holds (since (3.4) is a property of ℱ\mathcal{F}).

In Remark 4.3 we compute A,B,CA,B,C in terms of α,β\alpha,\beta. Let us mention that the converse of Lemma 4.1 has been investigated in [15, Theorem 3.1]. Let us mention here that the result [10, Lemma 2.1] is proved with a slightly different definition of John domains, but it was shown to be equivalent to Definition 1.6 in [50, Lemma 2.10]. Actually, the initial definition of John domains by John [39, Page 402] was even another one, but all definitions are equivalent according to the results of [44, Lemma 2.7] and [50, Lemma 2.10].

4.2. Proof of Theorem 1.7

We assume that 𝒳\mathcal{X} is a John domain and that 0<mρ≤ρ≤Mρ<+∞0<m_{\rho}\leq\rho\leq M_{\rho}<+\infty. In order to apply Theorem 3.6, we first verify that its assumptions are verified. Concerning the Boman chain condition, we already checked (3.3) and (3.4) in Section 4.1. The property (3.5) follows from (3.2) and the fact that Qj=σ​PjQ_{j}=\sigma P_{j}, together with the fact that 0<mρ≤ρ≤Mρ<+∞0<m_{\rho}\leq\rho\leq M_{\rho}<+\infty. These upper and lower bounds on ρ\rho also imply conditions (3.7) and (3.18). Therefore we may apply Theorem 3.6 in 𝒳\mathcal{X}, i.e., (3.19) holds. We consider this inequality for ψ0=ψμ\psi_{0}=\psi_{\mu} and ψ1=ψν\psi_{1}=\psi_{\nu}, which are both continuous in 𝒴\mathcal{Y}. Since (∇ψμ∗)#​ρ=μ(\nabla\psi_{\mu}^{*})_{\#}\rho=\mu and (∇ψν∗)#​ρ=ν(\nabla\psi_{\nu}^{*})_{\#}\rho=\nu we obtain

Varρ​(ϕμ−ϕν)≤C′​⟨ψμ−ψν|ν−μ⟩.{\rm Var}_{\rho}\left(\phi_{\mu}-\phi_{\nu}\right)\leq C^{\prime}\langle\psi_{\mu}-\psi_{\nu}|\nu-\mu\rangle. (4.3)

Then, one can check that ψμ−ψν\psi_{\mu}-\psi_{\nu} is diam⁡(𝒳){\rm diam}(\mathcal{X})-Lipschitz continuous, hence by the Kantorovich-Rubinstein duality formula for the W1W_{1} distance (see [54, Theorem 1.14]) the following upper bound for the right-hand side in (4.3) holds:

⟨ψμ−ψν|ν−μ⟩≤diam⁡(𝒳)​W1​(μ,ν).\langle\psi_{\mu}-\psi_{\nu}|\nu-\mu\rangle\leq{\rm diam}(\mathcal{X})W_{1}(\mu,\nu). (4.4)

Finally, we observe that Varρ​(ϕμ−ϕν)=‖ϕν−ϕν‖L2​(ρ)2{\rm Var}_{\rho}(\phi_{\mu}-\phi_{\nu})=\|\phi_{\nu}-\phi_{\nu}\|_{L^{2}(\rho)}^{2} since ∫𝒳ϕμ​𝑑ρ=∫𝒳ϕν​𝑑ρ=0\int_{\mathcal{X}}\phi_{\mu}d\rho=\int_{\mathcal{X}}\phi_{\nu}d\rho=0. All in all, putting (4.3) and (4.4) together, we have obtained (1.9), i.e., the stability of Brenier potentials.

Like for the log-concave case, the stability of Brenier maps (1.10) now follows from Proposition 2.2. Since u=ϕμu=\phi_{\mu} and v=ϕνv=\phi_{\nu} are R𝒴R_{\mathcal{Y}}-Lipschitz and convex in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}, and the boundary of ∂𝒳\partial\mathcal{X} is assumed rectifiable, (1.9) and Proposition 2.2 imply (1.10) since

Mρ−1/2∥Tμ−Tν∥L2​(ρ)\displaystyle M_{\rho}^{-1/2}\|T_{\mu}-T_{\nu}\|_{L^{2}(\rho)} ≤‖Tμ−Tν‖L2​(λ,𝒳)≤Cρ,𝒴​‖ϕμ−ϕν‖L2​(λ,𝒳)1/3\displaystyle\leq\|T_{\mu}-T_{\nu}\|_{L^{2}(\lambda,\mathcal{X})}\leq C_{\rho,\mathcal{Y}}\|\phi_{\mu}-\phi_{\nu}\|_{L^{2}(\lambda,\mathcal{X})}^{1/3}
≤Cρ,𝒴mρ−1/6∥ϕμ−ϕν∥L2​(ρ)1/3≤Cρ,𝒴mρ−1/6W1(μ,ν)1/6.\displaystyle\leq C_{\rho,\mathcal{Y}}m_{\rho}^{-1/6}\|\phi_{\mu}-\phi_{\nu}\|_{L^{2}(\rho)}^{1/3}\leq C_{\rho,\mathcal{Y}}m_{\rho}^{-1/6}W_{1}(\mu,\nu)^{1/6}. (4.5)
Remark 4.2.

As already mentioned, our proof of Lemma 3.3 is inspired by techniques developed in [9] (building upon anterior work [10]) to prove Poincaré-Sobolev inequalities in John domains. In both cases, a global variance is controlled by a sum of local variances.

For Sobolev-Poincaré inequalities, it is known [14, Theorem 1.1] that the property for a domain 𝒳⊂ℝd\mathcal{X}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} with finite volume to support Sobolev-Poincaré inequalities is almost equivalent to 𝒳\mathcal{X} being a John domain. The two properties are truly equivalent if 𝒳\mathcal{X} is assumed in addition to satisfy a separation condition described in [14], which is verified for instance for simply connected planar domains. Analogously, Theorem 1.9 hints towards an equivalence for a bounded domain 𝒳\mathcal{X} between the property that it is John (or some related property) and that the uniform probability density on 𝒳\mathcal{X} has the potential stability property. However, like for Sobolev-Poincaré inequalities, there are obvious caveats, which explain the need of a separation property for the equivalence to hold: for instance in dimension d≥2d\geq 2, it is possible to remove a countable number of points to a ball to make it a non-John domain, while the optimal transport potentials and maps with uniform source measure are unchanged (and therefore the stability property is unchanged under this operation).

Remark 4.3.

We proved that ρ\rho satisfies the Boman chain condition for some parameters A,B,CA,B,C. Let us briefly explain how to express these parameters in terms of the parameter α\alpha of the John domain 𝒳\mathcal{X} (see Definition 1.6). For this, we need to dig into Boman’s proof of Lemma 4.1 given in [10, Lemma 2.1]. Due to properties of the Whitney decomposition (Lemma 3.1) and the construction of the family of cubes in the Boman chain condition (see Section 4.1), we may take A=12dA=12^{d} and

C=(4σ−1)d​supQMρQmρQC=\left(\frac{4}{\sigma-1}\right)^{d}\sup_{Q}\frac{M_{\rho_{Q}}}{m_{\rho_{Q}}} (4.6)

which is finite because bounded above by (4σ−1)d​Mρmρ\left(\frac{4}{\sigma-1}\right)^{d}\frac{M_{\rho}}{m_{\rho}}. Both AA and CC are thus independent of α\alpha. The proof of [10, Lemma 2.1] gives B=40​dα′B=\frac{40d}{\alpha^{\prime}} if we take the same definition of John domains as Boman, i.e., dist⁡(γ⁡(t),∂𝒳)≥α′​|γ⁡(t)−x|{\rm dist}(\gamma(t),\partial\mathcal{X})\geq\alpha^{\prime}|\gamma(t)-x| instead of (1.8) (and the ratio of α\alpha and α′\alpha^{\prime} is bounded above and below according to [50, Lemma 2.10]). Also, recall that due to Theorem 2.1,

CDM=e​MρQmρQ​R𝒴​diam​(Q),C_{\rm DM}=e\frac{M_{\rho_{Q}}}{m_{\rho_{Q}}}R_{\mathcal{Y}}{\rm diam}(Q), (4.7)

which is uniformly bounded above by e​Mρmρ​R𝒴​diam​(𝒳)e\frac{M_{\rho}}{m_{\rho}}R_{\mathcal{Y}}{\rm diam}(\mathcal{X}). Therefore the constants Cρ,𝒴C_{\rho,\mathcal{Y}} in (1.9) and (1.10) are totally explicit.

4.3. Extension to finite unions of John domains

In this section, we show that optimal transport maps are still stable if one replaces in Theorem 1.7 the assumption that 𝒳\mathcal{X} is a John domain by the assumption that 𝒳\mathcal{X} is a finite union of John domains. On the side of Brenier potentials, we observed in Section 3.3 that they are not unique as soon as 𝒳\mathcal{X} has at least two connected components separated by a positive distance, but the proof of the proposition below shows that stability of Brenier potentials can be recovered by shifting them by an appropriate constant on each connected component, see (4.9) below.

Proposition 4.4.

Let 𝒳=J1∪…∪Jk⊂ℝd\mathcal{X}=J_{1}\cup\ldots\cup J_{k}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} be a finite union of John domains JiJ_{i} whose closures pairwise do not intersect, and with rectifiable boundaries. Let ρ\rho be a probability density on 𝒳\mathcal{X}, bounded from above and below by positive constants. Then, for any compact set 𝒴\mathcal{Y}, there exists Cρ,𝒴>0C_{\rho,\mathcal{Y}}>0 such that for any probability measures μ,ν\mu,\nu supported in 𝒴\mathcal{Y},

‖Tμ−Tν‖L2​(ρ)≤Cρ,𝒴​W1​(μ,ν)16.\|T_{\mu}-T_{\nu}\|_{L^{2}(\rho)}\leq C_{\rho,\mathcal{Y}}W_{1}(\mu,\nu)^{\frac{1}{6}}. (4.8)
Proof.

Denote by Tμ=∇ϕμT_{\mu}=\nabla\phi_{\mu} and Tν=∇ϕνT_{\nu}=\nabla\phi_{\nu} the optimal transports from ρ\rho to μ,ν\mu,\nu. The functions ϕμ\phi_{\mu} and ϕν\phi_{\nu} are convex according to Brenier’s theorem, but in this proof (and only here) we do not assume ∫𝒳ϕμ​𝑑ρ=∫𝒳ϕν​𝑑ρ=0\int_{\mathcal{X}}\phi_{\mu}d\rho=\int_{\mathcal{X}}\phi_{\nu}d\rho=0.

We consider ρi\rho_{i} the restriction of ρ\rho to JiJ_{i}. We denote by ρ~i=ρi/ρi​(Ji)\tilde{\rho}_{i}=\rho_{i}/\rho_{i}(J_{i}) the associated probability density. According to Theorem 3.6, for any ψ0,ψ1∈𝒞0​(𝒴)\psi_{0},\psi_{1}\in\mathcal{C}^{0}(\mathcal{Y}),

Varρ~i(ψ1∗−ψ0∗)≤Cρ,𝒴⟨ψ1−ψ0∣∇ψ0​#∗ρ~i−∇ψ1​#∗ρ~i⟩{\rm Var}_{\tilde{\rho}_{i}}(\psi_{1}^{*}-\psi_{0}^{*})\leq C_{\rho,\mathcal{Y}}\langle\psi_{1}-\psi_{0}\mid\nabla\psi_{0\#}^{*}\tilde{\rho}_{i}-\nabla\psi_{1\#}^{*}\tilde{\rho}_{i}\rangle

Applying this inequality to ψ0=ϕμ∗\psi_{0}=\phi_{\mu}^{*} and ψ1=ϕν∗\psi_{1}=\phi_{\nu}^{*}, and multiplying by ρi​(Ji)\rho_{i}(J_{i}) on both sides, we obtain

ρi(Ji)Varρ~i(ϕμ−ϕν)≤Cρ,𝒴⟨ϕν∗−ϕμ∗∣∇ϕμ​#ρi−∇ϕν​#ρi⟩.\rho_{i}(J_{i}){\rm Var}_{\tilde{\rho}_{i}}(\phi_{\mu}-\phi_{\nu})\leq C_{\rho,\mathcal{Y}}\langle\phi_{\nu}^{*}-\phi_{\mu}^{*}\mid\nabla\phi_{\mu\#}\rho_{i}-\nabla\phi_{\nu\#}\rho_{i}\rangle.

Let ci=∫𝒳(ϕμ−ϕν)​d​ρ~ic_{i}=\int_{\mathcal{X}}(\phi_{\mu}-\phi_{\nu})d\tilde{\rho}_{i}. Then summing the above inequality over ii we deduce

∑i=1k∥ϕμ−ϕν−ci∥L2​(ρi)2≤Cρ,𝒴⟨ϕν∗−ϕμ∗∣∇ϕμ​#ρ−∇ϕν​#ρ⟩≤Cρ,𝒴W1(μ,ν).\sum_{i=1}^{k}\|\phi_{\mu}-\phi_{\nu}-c_{i}\|_{L^{2}(\rho_{i})}^{2}\leq C_{\rho,\mathcal{Y}}\langle\phi_{\nu}^{*}-\phi_{\mu}^{*}\mid\nabla\phi_{\mu\#}\rho-\nabla\phi_{\nu\#}\rho\rangle\leq C_{\rho,\mathcal{Y}}W_{1}(\mu,\nu). (4.9)

where in the last inequality we used Kantorovich-Rubinstein duality. To get stability of maps we apply Proposition 2.2 in JiJ_{i}, which gives

‖Tμ−Tν‖L2​(ρi)2≤Cρ,𝒴​‖ϕμ−ϕν−ci‖L2​(ρi)2/3.\|T_{\mu}-T_{\nu}\|_{L^{2}(\rho_{i})}^{2}\leq C_{\rho,\mathcal{Y}}\|\phi_{\mu}-\phi_{\nu}-c_{i}\|_{L^{2}(\rho_{i})}^{2/3}.

Summing over ii we get

‖Tμ−Tν‖L2​(ρ)2≤Cρ,𝒴​∑i=1k‖ϕμ−ϕν−ci‖L2​(ρi)2/3≤Cρ,𝒴,k​(∑i=1k‖ϕμ−ϕν−ci‖L2​(ρi)2)1/3\|T_{\mu}-T_{\nu}\|_{L^{2}(\rho)}^{2}\leq C_{\rho,\mathcal{Y}}\sum_{i=1}^{k}\|\phi_{\mu}-\phi_{\nu}-c_{i}\|_{L^{2}(\rho_{i})}^{2/3}\leq C_{\rho,\mathcal{Y},k}\Bigl(\sum_{i=1}^{k}\|\phi_{\mu}-\phi_{\nu}-c_{i}\|_{L^{2}(\rho_{i})}^{2}\Bigr)^{1/3} (4.10)

where we used ∑i=1kai≤k2/3​(∑i=1kai3)1/3\sum_{i=1}^{k}a_{i}\leq k^{2/3}\Bigl(\sum_{i=1}^{k}a_{i}^{3}\Bigr)^{1/3} for any ai≥0a_{i}\geq 0, which is a consequence of Hölder’s inequality. Combining (4.9) and (4.10) we obtain (4.8). ∎

Remark 4.5.

It is explained in [42, Section 3.5] that similar stability bounds still hold if the source ρ\rho is bounded above and below on a domain with an infinite number of connected components, as soon as the measure of the connected components decays sufficiently quickly (when they are non-increasingly ordered).

4.4. Proof of Theorem 1.10

The proof of Theorem 1.10 follows broadly the same lines as that of Theorem 1.7. Again we first need to check that the assumptions of Theorem 3.6 are verified.

Let us observe that due to (1.11) and (4.2), there exists E>0E>0 such that if Q∈ℱQ\in\mathcal{F} and x,y∈Qx,y\in Q, then E−1​ρ​(y)≤ρ⁡(x)≤E​ρ​(y)E^{-1}\rho(y)\leq\rho(x)\leq E\rho(y). This proves (3.18). Now let us check the Boman chain condition. The above observation also implies that if Q,Q′Q,Q^{\prime} intersect, then E−2​ρ​(y)≤ρ⁡(x)≤E2​ρ​(y)E^{-2}\rho(y)\leq\rho(x)\leq E^{2}\rho(y) for any x∈Qx\in Q and y∈Q′y\in Q^{\prime}. Therefore, denoting by λ\lambda the Lebesgue measure in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d},

E−2​λ⁡(Q)λ⁡(Q′)≤ρ⁡(Q)ρ⁡(Q′)≤E2​λ⁡(Q)λ⁡(Q′)E^{-2}\frac{\lambda(Q)}{\lambda(Q^{\prime})}\leq\frac{\rho(Q)}{\rho(Q^{\prime})}\leq E^{2}\frac{\lambda(Q)}{\lambda(Q^{\prime})}

and

ρ⁡(Q∩Q′)max⁡(ρ⁡(Q),ρ⁡(Q′))≥E−2​λ⁡(Q∩Q′)max⁡(λ⁡(Q),λ⁡(Q′)).\frac{\rho(Q\cap Q^{\prime})}{\max(\rho(Q),\rho(Q^{\prime}))}\geq E^{-2}\frac{\lambda(Q\cap Q^{\prime})}{\max(\lambda(Q),\lambda(Q^{\prime}))}.

Now (3.5) can be deduced as follows. Recall that each Boman cube is obtained as σ​P\sigma P where PP is a cube of the Whitney decomposition (see Section 4.1). Moreover, any two consecutive cubes in the Boman chains used to prove Lemma 4.1 are scalings of Whitney cubes sharing part of their boundary. One can see this directly from the proof in [10, Lemma 2.1], but this property also follows from the fact that if two Boman cubes Q=σ​PQ=\sigma P and Q′=σ​P′Q^{\prime}=\sigma P^{\prime} have non-empty intersection, then the original cubes PP and P′P^{\prime} have touching boundaries. The latter fact can be proved by contradiction: if the boundaries of PP and P′P^{\prime} do not touch, assume without loss of generality ℓ⁡(P)≥ℓ⁡(P′)\ell(P)\geq\ell(P^{\prime}); then all Whitney cubes sharing part of their boundary with PP are of sidelength ≥ℓ⁡(P)/4\geq\ell(P)/4 due to (3.2) (and they are different from P′P^{\prime}), hence there exists at least one coordinate axis along which PP and P′P^{\prime} are separated by at least ℓ⁡(P)/4\ell(P)/4. The projections of the scalings QQ and Q′Q^{\prime} along this coordinate axis are also at strictly positive distance (since σ≤10/9\sigma\leq 10/9), which shows that Q∩Q′=∅Q\cap Q^{\prime}=\emptyset. Using again (3.2), we deduce that (3.5) holds. The other two conditions (3.3) and (3.4) of the Boman chain condition have already been checked in Section 4.1. There remains to prove that (3.7) holds:

Lemma 4.6.

The doubling condition (3.7) holds for some D<+∞D<+\infty.

𝒳ε={x∈𝒳∣d⁡(x,∂𝒳)≤ε}\mathcal{X}_{\varepsilon}=\{x\in\mathcal{X}\mid d(x,\partial\mathcal{X})\leq\varepsilon\}

4.5. Proof of Theorem 1.11

The proof of Theorem 1.11 follows the same lines as that of Theorem 1.10. Again we check that the assumptions of Theorem 3.6 are satisfied. For (3.18) and the Boman chain condition, the argument is exactly the same as at the beginning of Section 4.4, we do not repeat it here. We only need to verify the doubling condition (3.7).

The doubling condition (3.7) is verified for some D<+∞D<+\infty.

again due to the fact that Q⊂B⁡(0,3​η)Q\subset B(0,3\eta) and then (4.2). This proves that the doubling condition is verified. ∎

Therefore Theorem 3.6 applies, and the stability of Brenier potentials (1.14) follows via Kantorovich-Rubinstein duality (4.4) as in Section 4.2.

For the stability of maps (1.15), we set Kε=B⁡(0,1)∖B⁡(0,ε)K_{\varepsilon}=B(0,1)\setminus B(0,\varepsilon) and ρε=ρ|Kε\rho_{\varepsilon}=\rho_{|K_{\varepsilon}}. ≤Cd,𝒴​Mρε​‖ϕμ−ϕν‖L2​(ρ)2/3\displaystyle\leq C_{d,\mathcal{Y}}M_{\rho_{\varepsilon}}\|\phi_{\mu}-\phi_{\nu}\|_{L^{2}(\rho)}^{2/3}
≤Cd,𝒴​ε1−d​W1​(μ,ν)1/3.\displaystyle\leq C_{d,\mathcal{Y}}\varepsilon^{1-d}W_{1}(\mu,\nu)^{1/3}.

Remark 4.8.

The assumptions of Theorems 1.10 and 1.11 are the simplest ones which guarantee: (i) the Boman chain property (3.5); (ii) the boundedness of the maximal operator MM defined in Appendix A; (iii) property (4.13); (iv) an estimate of mρεm_{\rho_{\varepsilon}} and/or MρεM_{\rho_{\varepsilon}} as a power of ε\varepsilon. Theorem 1.10 would hold for any other family of ρ\rho’s for which the above four ingredients can be proved.

5. Proof of Theorem 1.9: counterexample to Hölder potential stability

We first prove the result for d=2d=2. The coordinates in ℝ2\mathbb{R}^{2} are denoted by x1,x2x_{1},x_{2}. We recall the concept of room and passage domain (see [2], [23, pp. 521-523] for instance). Figure 1 illustrates our description. Take a sequence of rooms (i.e., rectangles) RjR_{j}, contained in the unit ball of ℝ2\mathbb{R}^{2}, j∈ℕ∗j\in\mathbb{N}^{*}, RjR_{j} symmetric with respect to the x1x_{1}-axis, and such that Rj¯∩Rk¯=∅\overline{R_{j}}\cap\overline{R_{k}}=\emptyset for j≠kj\neq k. These rooms are labelled as R1,R2,…R_{1},R_{2},\ldots along the increasing x1x_{1}-axis. They are joined together by passages (i.e., rectangles) PnP_{n}, n∈ℕ∗n\in\mathbb{N}^{*}, PnP_{n} symmetric with respect to the x1x_{1}-axis, of height hnh_{n} much smaller than the height of the adjoining rooms RnR_{n} and Rn+1R_{n+1}. In particular the whole room and passage domain is contained in the unit ball. The passages PnP_{n} are also ordered as P1,P2,…P_{1},P_{2},\ldots along the increasing x1x_{1}-axis. The sidelengths and centers of all these rectangles will be specified later.

We denote by tnt_{n} (resp. tn′t_{n}^{\prime}) the infimum (resp. the supremum) of the abscissa x1x_{1} in PnP_{n}. In particular, tn<tn′<tn+1t_{n}<t_{n}^{\prime}<t_{n+1} for any n∈ℕ∗n\in\mathbb{N}^{*}. We fix the parameters tn,tn′t_{n},t_{n}^{\prime} and the rectangles RnR_{n} for n∈ℕ∗n\in\mathbb{N}^{*}. Then, the heights hnh_{n} are chosen sufficiently small, in order to satisfy the following property: for any δ>0\delta>0,

limn→+∞hnδ|tn−tn′|2​λ​(Rn+1)=0\lim_{n\rightarrow+\infty}\frac{h_{n}^{\delta}}{|t_{n}-t_{n}^{\prime}|^{2}\lambda(R_{n+1})}=0 (5.1)

where λ\lambda denotes the Lebesgue measure in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}. We denote by 𝒳\mathcal{X} the room and passage domain given by the union of all RnR_{n}’s and PnP_{n}’s, for n≥1n\geq 1. Finally, let ρ\rho denote a probability density on 𝒳\mathcal{X} bounded away from 00 and +∞+\infty, i.e., there exist mρ>0m_{\rho}>0 and Mρ<+∞M_{\rho}<+\infty such that mρ≤ρ≤Mρm_{\rho}\leq\rho\leq M_{\rho} in 𝒳\mathcal{X}. For instance, one can take ρ\rho to be the normalized Lebesgue measure on the room and passage domain.

Consider the convex functions ϕn​(x)=|x1−tn|\phi_{n}(x)=|x_{1}-t_{n}| and ϕn′​(x)=|x1−tn′|\phi_{n}^{\prime}(x)=|x_{1}-t_{n}^{\prime}|, which are the respective Brenier potentials for the quadratic transport from ρ\rho to (∇ϕn)#​ρ(\nabla\phi_{n})_{\#}\rho, and from ρ\rho to (∇ϕn′)#​ρ(\nabla\phi_{n}^{\prime})_{\#}\rho. For x=(x1,x2)∈ℝ2x=(x_{1},x_{2})\in\mathbb{R}^{2},

ϕn′​(x)−ϕn​(x)={tn′−tn​ if ​x1≤tntn−tn′​ if ​x1≥tn′\phi_{n}^{\prime}(x)-\phi_{n}(x)=\begin{cases}t_{n}^{\prime}-t_{n}\text{ if }x_{1}\leq t_{n}\\ t_{n}-t_{n}^{\prime}\text{ if }x_{1}\geq t_{n}^{\prime}\end{cases} (5.2)

and

|ϕn′​(x)−ϕn​(x)|≤|tn−tn′|​ if ​x∈Pn.|\phi_{n}^{\prime}(x)-\phi_{n}(x)|\leq|t_{n}-t_{n}^{\prime}|\text{ if }x\in P_{n}. (5.3)

Consequently,

We set

vn=ρ⁡({x∈𝒳∣x1≤tn})andwn=ρ⁡({x∈𝒳∣x1≥tn′}).v_{n}=\rho(\{x\in\mathcal{X}\mid x_{1}\leq t_{n}\})\qquad\text{and}\qquad w_{n}=\rho(\{x\in\mathcal{X}\mid x_{1}\geq t_{n}^{\prime}\}).

We have vn→1v_{n}\rightarrow 1, wn→0w_{n}\rightarrow 0 and ρ⁡(Pn)→0\rho(P_{n})\rightarrow 0 as n→+∞n\rightarrow+\infty. Besides, there holds for any n∈ℕ∗n\in\mathbb{N}^{*}

vn+wn+ρ⁡(Pn)=1.v_{n}+w_{n}+\rho(P_{n})=1. (5.4)

=(1−2​wn)​(tn′−tn)\displaystyle=(1-2w_{n})(t_{n}^{\prime}-t_{n})

where the last equality comes from (5.4). Hence, still for nn large enough,

≥(tn′−tn)2​(1−ρ⁡(Pn)−(1−2​wn)2)\displaystyle\geq(t_{n}^{\prime}-t_{n})^{2}(1-\rho(P_{n})-(1-2w_{n})^{2})

since wn→0w_{n}\rightarrow 0 and wn≥ρ⁡(Rn+1)w_{n}\geq\rho(R_{n+1}).

Fix p∈[1,+∞)p\in[1,+\infty). Let us compute Wp​(μn,μn′)W_{p}(\mu_{n},\mu_{n}^{\prime}) for n∈ℕ∗n\in\mathbb{N}^{*}.
