The subset of 𝒳\mathcal{X} given by the points x∈𝒳x\in\mathcal{X} such that ∇ϕn​(x)≠∇ϕn′​(x)\nabla\phi_{n}(x)\neq\nabla\phi_{n}^{\prime}(x) is exactly PnP_{n}. Since dist⁡(A,B)=2{\rm dist}(A,B)=2 we deduce Wp​(μn,μn′)=2​ρ​(Pn)1/pW_{p}(\mu_{n},\mu_{n}^{\prime})=2\rho(P_{n})^{1/p}.

Now we observe that ρ⁡(Pn)≤Mρ​λ​(𝒳)−1​hn​|tn′−tn|≤hn\rho(P_{n})\leq M_{\rho}\lambda(\mathcal{X})^{-1}h_{n}|t_{n}^{\prime}-t_{n}|\leq h_{n} for nn large enough where hnh_{n} denotes the height of PnP_{n} and λ\lambda denotes the Lebesgue measure in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}. Due to (5.1), ρ⁡(Pn)≤hn≤ρ⁡(Rn+1)/2\rho(P_{n})\leq h_{n}\leq\rho(R_{n+1})/2 for nn large enough. Plugging into (5.5) we get that for any q>0q>0 and p∈[1,+∞)p\in[1,+\infty), for nn large enough,

Wp​(μn,μn′)qVarρ​(ϕn−ϕn′)≤2q+1​mρ​hnq/p|tn−tn′|2​λ​(Rn+1)​⟶n→+∞​0\frac{W_{p}(\mu_{n},\mu_{n}^{\prime})^{q}}{{\rm Var}_{\rho}(\phi_{n}-\phi_{n}^{\prime})}\leq 2^{q+1}m_{\rho}\frac{h_{n}^{q/p}}{|t_{n}-t_{n}^{\prime}|^{2}\lambda(R_{n+1})}\underset{n\rightarrow+\infty}{\longrightarrow}0

which concludes the proof when d=2d=2. The generalization to any d≥2d\geq 2 is straightforward, considering hyperrectangles rooms and passages, instead of rectangles. Notice that in our example the target measures μn,μn′\mu_{n},\mu_{n}^{\prime} are supported in the closure of the unit ball of ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}, but the result actually holds for any fixed non-empty ball B⁡(0,r)⊂ℝdB(0,r)\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} (supporting the target measures), by considering ϕn=12​r​|x−tn|\phi_{n}=\frac{1}{2}r|x-t_{n}| and ϕn′=12​r​|x−tn′|\phi_{n}^{\prime}=\frac{1}{2}r|x-t_{n}^{\prime}|.

Remark 5.1.

From the above construction it is straightforward to construct a 1d probability density ρ\rho on ℝ\mathbb{R}, whose support is a compact interval, and for which the Hölder stability property of Definition 1.8 does not hold. Let π:ℝ2→ℝ\pi:\mathbb{R}^{2}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}, π⁡(x1,x2)=x1\pi(x_{1},x_{2})=x_{1} be the projection onto the first coordinate. Consider the 1d probability measure ρ′=π#​ρ\rho^{\prime}=\pi_{\#}\rho on ℝ\mathbb{R}, where ρ\rho is the normalized Lebesgue measure on the domain constructed above (and represented in Figure 1). Then the above computations show that the Brenier potentials associated to ρ′\rho^{\prime} do not satisfy the Hölder potential stability property. However, the Brenier maps with source measure ρ′\rho^{\prime} are stable: even better, they satisfy ‖Tμ−Tν‖L2​(ρ′)=W2​(μ,ν)\|T_{\mu}-T_{\nu}\|_{L^{2}(\rho^{\prime})}=W_{2}(\mu,\nu), this equality being a property of all 1d probability measure.

Remark 5.2.

There exist other counterexamples to Hölder potential stability than room and passage domains, for instance domains with a sharp outward cusp: in ℝ2\mathbb{R}^{2}, consider a domain contained in the half-plane x1≥0x_{1}\geq 0 of the form |x2|≤e−1/x12|x_{2}|\leq e^{-1/x_{1}^{2}} near 00, and a probability density ρ\rho on this domain, bounded above and below by positive constants. Then the same family of potentials |x1−t||x_{1}-t| as above shows that Hölder potential stability does not hold in this case either.

6. Proof of Theorem 1.12: generalized Cauchy distributions

We describe in Section 6.1 a natural attempt to prove Theorem 1.12 which, although too rough to lead to a complete proof, gives clear insights about a key difficulty of the problem. Our final proof is an improvement over this attempt. Its broad lines are described at the end of Section 6.1.

6.1. Warm-up and proof strategy

In this section, which is merely illustrative, we assume for simplicity that ρ⁡(x)=cβ​⟨x⟩−β\rho(x)=c_{\beta}\langle x\rangle^{-\beta} with β>d+2\beta>d+2, and cβ>0c_{\beta}>0 is a normalizing constant. We explain one of the key difficulties of the proof in this simple case. A natural approach would be to apply Theorem 2.1, but since it works only in bounded sets, we are naturally led to truncate the source measure ρ\rho, as in the log-concave case handled in Section 2.2. For r≥0r\geq 0, recall that ℬr=B⁡(0,r)⊂ℝd\mathcal{B}_{r}=B(0,r)\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} denotes the closed Euclidean ball of center 00 and radius rr. We denote by ϕμ,r\phi_{\mu,r} (resp. ϕν,r\phi_{\nu,r}) the restriction of ϕμ\phi_{\mu} (resp. ϕν\phi_{\nu}) to ℬr\mathcal{B}_{r}, and we consider the probability measures

ρr=ρ|ℬrρ⁡(ℬr),μr=(∇ϕμ,r)#​ρr,νr=(∇ϕν,r)#​ρr.\rho_{r}=\frac{\rho_{|\mathcal{B}_{r}}}{\rho(\mathcal{B}_{r})},\qquad\mu_{r}=(\nabla\phi_{\mu,r})_{\#}\rho_{r},\qquad\nu_{r}=(\nabla\phi_{\nu,r})_{\#}\rho_{r}. (6.1)

Finally we set ψμ,r=ϕμ,r∗\psi_{\mu,r}=\phi_{\mu,r}^{*} and ψν,r=ϕν,r∗\psi_{\nu,r}=\phi_{\nu,r}^{*}. Simple arguments similar to (2.21) based on the fact that ϕμ,r\phi_{\mu,r} and ϕν,r\phi_{\nu,r} are R𝒴R_{\mathcal{Y}}-Lipschitz imply that for large rr,

Varρ​(ϕμ−ϕν)≤Varρr​(ϕμ,r−ϕν,r)+Cd,𝒴​rd+2−β.{\rm Var}_{\rho}(\phi_{\mu}-\phi_{\nu})\leq{\rm Var}_{\rho_{r}}(\phi_{\mu,r}-\phi_{\nu,r})+C_{d,\mathcal{Y}}r^{d+2-\beta}.

Since ℬr\mathcal{B}_{r} is a bounded convex domain on which ρ\rho is bounded from above and below, Theorem 2.1 yields

Varρr​(ϕμ,r−ϕν,r)≤Cd,𝒴​rβ+1​⟨ψμ,r−ψν,r|νr−μr⟩.{\rm Var}_{\rho_{r}}(\phi_{\mu,r}-\phi_{\nu,r})\leq C_{d,\mathcal{Y}}\ r^{\beta+1}\langle\psi_{\mu,r}-\psi_{\nu,r}|\nu_{r}-\mu_{r}\rangle. (6.2)

Now we observe that ψμ,r−ψν,r\psi_{\mu,r}-\psi_{\nu,r} is 2​r2r-Lipschitz (because diam⁡(ℬr)=2​r{\rm diam}(\mathcal{B}_{r})=2r) hence using Kantorovich-Rubinstein duality in the right-hand side of (6.2) we obtain

Varρ​(ϕμ−ϕν)≤Cd,𝒴​rd+2−β+Cd,𝒴​rβ+2​W1​(μr,νr).{\rm Var}_{\rho}(\phi_{\mu}-\phi_{\nu})\leq C_{d,\mathcal{Y}}\ r^{d+2-\beta}+C_{d,\mathcal{Y}}\ r^{\beta+2}W_{1}(\mu_{r},\nu_{r}). (6.3)

There remains to find an upper bound for W1​(μr,νr)W_{1}(\mu_{r},\nu_{r}) in terms of W1​(μ,ν)W_{1}(\mu,\nu). The best we can hope for is that for large rr,

W1​(μr,νr)≤W1​(μ,ν)+C𝒴​rd−βW_{1}(\mu_{r},\nu_{r})\leq W_{1}(\mu,\nu)+C_{\mathcal{Y}}\ r^{d-\beta}

(due to (2.22)). Plugging into (6.3) we see that the remainder term is too large to obtain (1.6), the method needs to be refined.

However, this strategy tells us that a key point is to be able to establish in ℬr\mathcal{B}_{r} a variance inequality like (6.2) with an improved dependence in rr. This is precisely what we do in our proof of Theorem 1.12. It relies on the same basic idea as Theorem 1.7, that of decomposing 𝒳\mathcal{X} (here, ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}) into convex sets Q∈ℱQ\in\mathcal{F}, and we do this in a way that the ratio MρQ/mρQM_{\rho_{Q}}/m_{\rho_{Q}} of the maximum density over the minimum density in each convex set QQ is bounded above uniformly in Q∈ℱQ\in\mathcal{F}. Then we apply the variance inequality in each QQ, and finally we glue together all these local variance inequalities to obtain a global one.

To do the gluing, it does not seem possible to adapt the strategy used to prove Theorem 1.7, namely to apply a Boman chain-type argument in ℬr\mathcal{B}_{r} (and then letting r→+∞r\rightarrow+\infty). Therefore, in the sequel, we follow a different strategy, which is based on the construction and the spectral analysis of a graph. We construct a decomposition of ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} into convex sets, and each of them is seen as one vertex of an infinite graph, endowed with a weight corresponding to its mass. The edges of this graph are given by those pairs of convex sets which intersect, and each edge is endowed with a weight equal to the mass of the intersection of the two convex sets. Then, the gluing argument for variance inequalities is obtained through a Cheeger inequality in finite truncations of the weighted graph that we just described. Using the Cheeger inequality is a robust strategy, with which it is possible for instance to recover Theorem 1.7 (at least in Lipschitz domains), and this is why we use it here; we briefly explain in Remark 6.9 an alternative argument to replace the part of the proof where the Cheeger inequality is used, but which is quite specific to the power law case considered in Theorem 1.12 and does not seem to generalize well.

6.2. Laplacians in weighted graphs and Cheeger inequality

We gather in this section general facts regarding Laplacians in infinite weighted graphs and the associated Cheeger inequality. Our presentation follows closely [6].

6.2.1. Weighted graphs

Let VV be a countable set equipped with the discrete topology. Elements of VV are called vertices. We assume that VV is endowed with a function δ:V→(0,∞)\delta:V\rightarrow(0,\infty) which can be turned into a Radon measure on VV of full support by the formula δ⁡(U)=∑i∈Uδi\delta(U)=\sum_{i\in U}\delta_{i} for U⊆VU\subseteq V (we denote by δi\delta_{i} the value of δ\delta at i∈Vi\in V). Then let w:V×V→[0,∞)w:V\times V\rightarrow[0,\infty) be a symmetric function vanishing on the diagonal and satisfying

∀i∈V,∑j∈Vwi​j<+∞\forall i\in V,\quad\sum_{j\in V}w_{ij}<+\infty

(here an in the sequel, wi​j=w⁡(i,j)w_{ij}=w(i,j)). We denote by EE the set of all edges, i.e., the set of all (i,j)∈V×V(i,j)\in V\times V such that wi​j>0w_{ij}>0. If (i,j)∈E(i,j)\in E, we say that ii and jj are neighbors. The weighted graph G=(V,E,δ,w)G=(V,E,\delta,w) is said locally finite if each vertex has only finitely many neighbors.

6.2.2. Graph Laplacians

Denote by Cc​(V)C_{c}(V) the space of real valued functions on VV with finite support. We set

ℓ2(V,δ)={u:V→ℝ∣∑i∈Vδiu(i)2<+∞}\ell^{2}(V,\delta)=\left\{u:V\rightarrow\mathbb{R}\mid\sum_{i\in V}\delta_{i}u(i)^{2}<+\infty\right\}

and endow it with the scalar product ⟨u,v⟩δ=∑i∈Vδi​u​(i)​v​(i)\langle u,v\rangle_{\delta}=\sum_{i\in V}\delta_{i}u(i)v(i) and the norm ‖u‖δ=⟨u,u⟩δ1/2\|u\|_{\delta}=\langle u,u\rangle_{\delta}^{1/2}. Let the quadratic form 𝒬=𝒬w\mathcal{Q}=\mathcal{Q}_{w} with domain 𝒟\mathcal{D} be given by

𝒬⁡(u)=12​∑i,j∈Vwi​j​(u⁡(i)−u⁡(j))2,𝒟={u∈ℓ2​(V,δ)∣𝒬⁡(u)<∞}.\mathcal{Q}(u)=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i,j\in V}w_{ij}(u(i)-u(j))^{2},\quad\mathcal{D}=\left\{u\in\ell^{2}(V,\delta)\mid\mathcal{Q}(u)<\infty\right\}.

The corresponding positive selfadjoint operator LL acts as

L​u​(i)=1δi​∑j∈Vwi​j​(u⁡(i)−u⁡(j))Lu(i)=\frac{1}{\delta_{i}}\sum_{j\in V}w_{ij}(u(i)-u(j)) (6.4)

(see [40, Theorem 1.12]). In the cases that will be considered in this paper,

∑i∈Vδi<+∞\sum_{i\in V}\delta_{i}<+\infty

and there exists C>0C>0 such that

∀i∈V,C​δi≥∑j∈Vwi​j.\forall i\in V,\quad C\delta_{i}\geq\sum_{j\in V}w_{ij}. (6.5)

As a consequence, LL is a bounded operator in ℓ2​(V,δ)\ell^{2}(V,\delta). Indeed,

|L​u​(i)|2≤δi−2​∑j∈Vwi​j​|u⁡(i)−u⁡(j)|2​∑j∈Vwi​j≤C​δi−1​∑j∈Vwi​j​|u⁡(i)−u⁡(j)|2|Lu(i)|^{2}\leq\delta_{i}^{-2}\sum_{j\in V}w_{ij}|u(i)-u(j)|^{2}\sum_{j\in V}w_{ij}\leq C\delta_{i}^{-1}\sum_{j\in V}w_{ij}|u(i)-u(j)|^{2}

hence

‖L​u‖δ2=∑i∈V|L​u​(i)|2​δi≤2​C​∑i,j∈Vwi​j​(|u⁡(i)|2+|u⁡(j)|2)=4​C​∑i,j∈Vwi​j​|u⁡(i)|2≤4​C​‖u‖δ2.\|Lu\|_{\delta}^{2}=\sum_{i\in V}|Lu(i)|^{2}\delta_{i}\leq 2C\sum_{i,j\in V}w_{ij}(|u(i)|^{2}+|u(j)|^{2})=4C\sum_{i,j\in V}w_{ij}|u(i)|^{2}\leq 4C\|u\|_{\delta}^{2}.

We notice that the function 𝟏∈𝒟\mathbf{1}\in\mathcal{D} equal to 11 on all VV is in the kernel of LL. We set

λ2(L)=inf{𝒬(u)∣∥u∥δ=1,⟨u,𝟏⟩δ=0}.\lambda_{2}(L)=\inf\{\mathcal{Q}(u)\mid\|u\|_{\delta}=1,\langle u,\mathbf{1}\rangle_{\delta}=0\}.

The Cheeger inequality is a lower bound on λ2​(L)\lambda_{2}(L) in terms of a constant measuring how well the graph is connected, called the isoperimetric constant of GG.

6.2.3. Isoperimetric constant and Cheeger inequality

For U⊂VU\subset V we denote by

vol​(U)=∑i∈Uδi\text{vol}(U)=\sum_{i\in U}\delta_{i}

its volume and by

|∂U|=∑i∈U,j∉Uwi​j|\partial U|=\sum_{i\in U,j\notin U}w_{ij} (6.6)

the size of its boundary. Finally the isoperimetric constant of GG is

h=infU⊂V0<vol⁡(U)≤12​vol​(V)|∂U|vol⁡(U).h=\inf_{\begin{subarray}{c}U\subset V\\ 0<{\rm vol}(U)\leq\frac{1}{2}{\rm vol}(V)\end{subarray}}\frac{|\partial U|}{{\rm vol}(U)}. (6.7)

The following Cheeger inequality will be instrumental.

Proposition 6.1.

If (6.5) holds, then λ2​(L)≥h2/2​C\lambda_{2}(L)\geq h^{2}/2C where CC is the constant in (6.5).

For completeness, we provide in Appendix B an elementary proof assuming that VV is finite, which is sufficient for the present paper since we apply Proposition 6.1 only to finite graphs (in Lemma 6.8). A proof of Proposition 6.1 for infinite graphs may be found in [49, Theorem 3.5]. A more general Cheeger inequality, applying as well to infinite graphs which do not verify (6.5) has been proved in [40, Theorem 13.4].

6.3. Gluing variance inequalities

Definition 6.2.

Let A,B<+∞A,B<+\infty. An absolutely continuous probability measure ρ⁡(x)​d​x\rho(x)dx on a bounded set 𝒳\mathcal{X} is said to be of type (A,B)(A,B) with respect to a finite family (Qi)i∈V(Q_{i})_{i\in V} of convex sets such that

spt⁡(ρ)=⋃i∈VQi{\rm spt}(\rho)=\bigcup_{i\in V}Q_{i} (6.8)

if the following properties are verified:

  1. (i)

    Each QiQ_{i} intersects at most AA of the sets QjQ_{j}’s, including itself.

    For any i∈Vi\in V,

    supx∈Qiρ|Qi(x)infx∈Qiρ|Qi(x)≤B.\frac{\sup_{x\in Q_{i}}\rho_{|Q_{i}}(x)}{\inf_{x\in Q_{i}}\rho_{|Q_{i}}(x)}\leq B. (6.9)

We simply say that ρ\rho is of type (A,B)(A,B) if it is of type (A,B)(A,B) with respect to some finite family (Qi)i∈V(Q_{i})_{i\in V} satisfying the above conditions.

To any probability measure of type (A,B)(A,B) it is possible to associate an undirected weighted graph as follows.

Definition 6.3 (Weighted graph associated to a measure of type (A,B)(A,B)).

To an absolutely continuous probability measure ρ\rho of type (A,B)(A,B) with respect to a finite family (Qi)i∈V(Q_{i})_{i\in V} we associate a weighted graph G=(V,E,δ,w)G=(V,E,\delta,w) as follows. Its vertices are given by the set VV, and each i∈Vi\in V has weight

δi=ρ⁡(Qi).\delta_{i}=\rho(Q_{i}).

The edges EE of GG are the couples (i,j)(i,j) for which wi​j>0w_{ij}>0 (and in particular i≠ji\neq j). Each edge (i,j)(i,j) is endowed with a weight

wi​j=ρ⁡(Qi∩Qj).w_{ij}=\rho(Q_{i}\cap Q_{j}).

The positive graph Laplacian LL on 𝒟⊂ℓ2​(V,δ)\mathcal{D}\subset\ell^{2}(V,\delta) acts as (6.4). The condition (6.5) is verified with C:=AC:=A.

6.4. Estimates for generalized Cauchy distributions

In the present section, assuming that ρ\rho is of the form

ρ⁡(x)=c⁡(x)​⟨x⟩−β,m≤c⁡(x)≤M,\rho(x)=c(x)\langle x\rangle^{-\beta},\qquad m\leq c(x)\leq M, (6.17)

we construct a decomposition of ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} into a family (Qi)i∈V(Q_{i})_{i\in V} of convex sets satisfying Definition 6.2, and we check all properties that will be needed to apply Theorem 6.4. As already mentioned in Section 6.1, it will be necessary to consider truncations ρr\rho_{r} of ρ\rho in order to apply Theorem 6.4, and therefore we consider for each rr a subfamily of (Qi)i∈V(Q_{i})_{i\in V} which covers the support of ρr\rho_{r}.

6.4.1. Decomposition of ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} and construction of a family of weighted graphs

Let ρ\rho be of the form (6.17). We construct a locally finite family (Qj)j∈V(Q_{j})_{j\in V} of subsets of ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} (depending on β\beta, omitted in the notation), indexed by V=ℕ×{−1,1}dV=\mathbb{N}\times\{-1,1\}^{d}. We refer the reader to Figure 2 for an illustration.

We set 𝒞0=B⁡(0,2)\mathcal{C}_{0}=B(0,2) and

𝒞J=B⁡(0,2J+1)∖B⁡(0,2J−1)\mathcal{C}_{J}=B(0,2^{J+1})\setminus B(0,2^{J-1}) (6.18)

for J∈ℕ∗J\in\mathbb{N}^{*}. There holds

ℝd=⋃J∈ℕ𝒞J.\mathbb{R}^{d}=\bigcup_{J\in\mathbb{N}}\mathcal{C}_{J}.

This is not a partition since some of the 𝒞J\mathcal{C}_{J} overlap, but any point in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} belongs to at most two of these sets. We consider the 2d2^{d} orthants

ℋσ={x∈ℝd∣∀i∈[d],σixi≥0}\mathcal{H}_{\sigma}=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\mid\forall i\in[d],\ \sigma_{i}x_{i}\geq 0\}

for σ=(σ1,…,σd)∈{−1,1}d\sigma=(\sigma_{1},\ldots,\sigma_{d})\in\{-1,1\}^{d}. We denote by Conv{\rm Conv} the convex-hull, and we finally define for (J,σ)∈ℕ∗×{−1,1}d(J,\sigma)\in\mathbb{N}^{*}\times\{-1,1\}^{d}

Q(J,σ)=Conv⁡(𝒞J∩ℋσ)Q_{(J,\sigma)}={\rm Conv}(\mathcal{C}_{J}\cap\mathcal{H}_{\sigma}) (6.19)

(which is included in the convex set ℋσ\mathcal{H}_{\sigma}) and Q(0,σ)=𝒞0=B⁡(0,2)Q_{(0,\sigma)}=\mathcal{C}_{0}=B(0,2) for any σ∈{−1,1}d\sigma\in\{-1,1\}^{d}.

We consider as in Definition 6.3 the graph G=(V,E,δ,w)G=(V,E,\delta,w) associated to the sets Q(J,σ)Q_{(J,\sigma)}. We could prove various properties of the graph GG, for instance that it has a positive spectral gap. But since we need later to perform a truncation of ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} in order to prove Theorem 1.4 (as explained in Section 6.1), we instead define a family of truncated graph depending on a parameter rr, and prove properties of this family which are “uniform in rr”.

We define this family of truncated graphs (i.e., subgraphs of GG) as follows, see Figure 3 for an illustration. For any r≥1r\geq 1 of the form r=2nr=2^{n} for some n∈ℕ∗n\in\mathbb{N}^{*}, Gr=(Vr,Er,δr,wr)G_{r}=(V_{r},E_{r},\delta_{r},w_{r}) is the restriction of G=(V,E,δ,w)G=(V,E,\delta,w) to the set of vertices (J,σ)∈V(J,\sigma)\in V such that Q(J,σ)⊂ℬrQ_{(J,\sigma)}\subset\mathcal{B}_{r}. The weights on the vertices VrV_{r} and edges ErE_{r} are unchanged compared to those on V,EV,E. Due to (6.18) and (6.19), for any r=2nr=2^{n},

ρr=ρ|ℬrρ⁡(ℬr)verifiesspt⁡(ρr)=⋃(J,σ)∈VrQ(J,σ).\rho_{r}=\frac{\rho_{|\mathcal{B}_{r}}}{\rho(\mathcal{B}_{r})}\quad\text{verifies}\quad{\rm spt}(\rho_{r})=\bigcup_{(J,\sigma)\in V_{r}}Q_{(J,\sigma)}.

In Section 6.5 we apply Theorem 6.4 to ρr\rho_{r} for rr large enough. For this, we prove here a uniform upper bound (independent of rr) on the constants A,BA,B appearing in the right-hand side of (6.10):

Lemma 6.6.

There exist A,B<+∞A,B<+\infty such that for any r=2nr=2^{n}, n∈ℕ∗n\in\mathbb{N}^{*}, ρr\rho_{r} is of type (A,B)(A,B) with respect to (Q(J,σ))(J,σ)∈Vr(Q_{(J,\sigma)})_{(J,\sigma)\in V_{r}}.

Let (J,σ)∈V(J,\sigma)\in V and assume J≠0J\neq 0 (for J=0J=0, the number of intersections with other sets is automatically bounded and (6.9) may be checked by hand). We observe that

Q(J,σ)⊂{x∈ℝd∣∑i=1dσixi≥2J−1}⊂ℝd∖B(0,d−1/22J−1)Q_{(J,\sigma)}\subset\Bigl\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\mid\sum_{i=1}^{d}\sigma_{i}x_{i}\geq 2^{J-1}\Bigr\}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d}\setminus B(0,d^{-1/2}2^{J-1})

hence

If Q(J,σ)Q_{(J,\sigma)} and Q(J′,σ′)Q_{(J^{\prime},\sigma^{\prime})} intersect for some (J′,σ′)∈V(J^{\prime},\sigma^{\prime})\in V, then due to (6.20), 2J′+1≥d−1/22J−12^{J^{\prime}+1}\geq d^{-1/2}2^{J-1} and 2J+1≥d−1/22J′−12^{J+1}\geq d^{-1/2}2^{J^{\prime}-1}. The number of such J′J^{\prime} is bounded above by 5+log2⁡(d)5+\log_{2}(d), hence the number of Q(J′,σ′)Q_{(J^{\prime},\sigma^{\prime})} intersecting Q(J,σ)Q_{(J,\sigma)} is at most 2d​(5+log2⁡(d))2^{d}(5+\log_{2}(d)), which is independent of (J,σ)∈V(J,\sigma)\in V and rr. Besides, (6.20) also implies that if x,y∈Q(J,σ)x,y\in Q_{(J,\sigma)}, then

ρ⁡(x)ρ⁡(y)≤Mm​(d−1/22J−1)−β(1+22​(J+1))−β/2≤Mm​(d−1/22J−1)−β2−β⁡(J+2)≤Mm​(8​d)β\frac{\rho(x)}{\rho(y)}\leq\frac{M}{m}\frac{(d^{-1/2}2^{J-1})^{-\beta}}{(1+2^{2(J+1)})^{-\beta/2}}\leq\frac{M}{m}\frac{(d^{-1/2}2^{J-1})^{-\beta}}{2^{-\beta(J+2)}}\leq\frac{M}{m}(8\sqrt{d})^{\beta}

Remark 6.11 (Stability estimates for exponentially decaying densities).

The proof strategy developed in this section may be adapted to prove stability estimates analogous to (1.16) and (1.17) in the case where ρ⁡(x)=c⁡(x)​e−κ​|x|−α\rho(x)=c(x)e^{-\kappa|x|^{-\alpha}} for α,κ>0\alpha,\kappa>0 and 0<m≤c⁡(x)≤M<+∞0<m\leq c(x)\leq M<+\infty. The main difference lies in the definition of the cells 𝒞J\mathcal{C}_{J}: instead of (6.18), we have to define the cells in a way that ρ\rho varies by not more than a multiplicative factor which is uniform over all cells. This can be made via a radial decomposition similar in spirit to (6.18). At the same time, in order for each cell to be convex and to intersect only a bounded number of other cells, an angular decomposition needs to be performed. The details are rather lengthy and we shall not pursue this here.

6.6. Weighted Poincaré inequalities

As a corollary of our proof technique, we recover weighted Poincaré inequalities for generalized Cauchy distributions similar to those established in the paper [8]:

Proposition 6.12.

Let ρ⁡(x)=c⁡(x)​⟨x⟩−β\rho(x)=c(x)\langle x\rangle^{-\beta} be a probability measure on ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}, with β>d+2\beta>d+2 and 0<m≤c⁡(x)≤M<+∞0<m\leq c(x)\leq M<+\infty. Then there exists C>0C>0 such that

Varρ​(f)≤C​∫ℝd|∇f​(x)|2​⟨x⟩2​𝑑ρ​(x){\rm Var}_{\rho}(f)\leq C\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}|\nabla f(x)|^{2}\langle x\rangle^{2}d\rho(x) (6.27)

for any function ff for which the right-hand side is finite.

Proof.

We notice that the QjQ_{j} constructed in Section 6.4.1 (and given by (6.19)) are obtained by homotheties and isometries of a single convex shape, namely the convex hull of the intersection of an orthant with an annulus whose outer radius is 44 times its inradius. As a consequence, the Poincaré-Wirtinger inequality Varρj​(f)≤Cj​∫Qj|∇f|2​d​ρj{\rm Var}_{\rho_{j}}(f)\leq C_{j}\int_{Q_{j}}|\nabla f|^{2}d\rho_{j} holds, with a constant CjC_{j} proportional to diam​(Qj)2{\rm diam}(Q_{j})^{2}. Due to the properties of the decomposition of ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} constructed in Section 6.4.1 this implies

Varρj​(f)≤C​∫Qj|∇f​(x)|2​⟨x⟩2​d​ρj​(x){\rm Var}_{\rho_{j}}(f)\leq C\int_{Q_{j}}|\nabla f(x)|^{2}\langle x\rangle^{2}d\rho_{j}(x)

with a constant CC which is now independent of jj (and ff). Applying Lemma 6.5 we obtain (6.27). ∎

The results in [8] derive such inequalities with other methods and address the dependence of CC in the parameters β,d\beta,d.

6.7. Comparison between gluing methods

It is worth comparing the two methods used in this work to glue together variance inequalities. The first one, based on the Boman chain condition, does not seem to generalize to unbounded supports, see comments in Section 6.1. On the contrary, the method based on spectral graph theory used in Section 6 could as well be used to prove stability for ρ\rho supported in a bounded domain 𝒳\mathcal{X}, by constructing the weighted graph associated to the Boman decomposition of 𝒳\mathcal{X} (with one vertex per cube and one edge per pair of intersecting cubes). However, proving that the Cheeger constant of this graph is >0>0 quickly becomes a pain unless assuming some stronger regularity on ∂𝒳\partial\mathcal{X}, for instance that 𝒳\mathcal{X} is a Lipschitz domain. This approach yields no improvement over Theorem 1.7 but it could be leveraged to find other cases than Theorems 1.10 and 1.11 where stability estimates can be proved even though ρ\rho is not assumed to be bounded away from 00 and +∞+\infty. We leave this for future work.

Let us finally illustrate on a simple example an interesting feature shared by both approaches. Let us consider a bounded domain 𝒳\mathcal{X} with dumbbell shape, i.e. two dsjoint balls joint by a thin tube of length 11 and radius ε≪1\varepsilon\ll 1. We endow 𝒳\mathcal{X} with the Lebesgue measure, normalized to be a probability measure. Then BB in Definition 3.2 is of order ε−1≫1\varepsilon^{-1}\gg 1, and DD in (3.7) is consequently ≳ε−d\gtrsim\varepsilon^{-d}. If one now considers the graph associated to the Boman cube decomposition of 𝒳\mathcal{X}, then one can check that λ2≲εd+1\lambda_{2}\lesssim\varepsilon^{d+1}. In both cases we see that the constants in the variance inequalities (3.19) and (6.10) blow-up as ε→0\varepsilon\rightarrow 0. Of course, this is related to the worsening of the Poincaré constant of 𝒳\mathcal{X} as ε→0\varepsilon\rightarrow 0.
